title: Deblurring images, in Python
text:
Preface
These nine chapters teach how to restore a blurred image, from the first principles to the edge of a research project. They accompany a textbook,
which teaches with MATLAB. Here the same mathematics is taught in Python, in our own words, and every chapter ends on real data: narrowband images of the Eagle Nebula (M16) taken with a 14 cm refractor, with Hubble Space Telescope images of the same field as a reference.
This is a companion, not a substitute. Read the chapter of the book, then work through the corresponding chapter here.

title: Deblurring images, in Python
text:
Contents
The book, chapter by chapter

The image deblurring problem: why the obvious solution fails.
Images as arrays: NumPy in place of MATLAB; display is not data.
The blurring function: the PSF, measured on a star; noise; boundaries.
Structured computations: never building the matrix.
The SVD and spectral analysis: the Picard plot.
Regularisation by spectral filtering: Tikhonov, and how much of it.
Colour images and smoothing norms: beyond the basic method.

Towards the research project

From one frame to many: proper coaddition.
Iterative methods: when there is no closed form; robust coaddition.

followed by the references and a listing of the helper module.
Chapters 1 to 7 follow the seven chapters of Hansen et al. (2006). Chapter 8 is not in that book: it extends the method from one image to many, which is the situation of every astronomer, and introduces proper coaddition (Zackay and Ofek 2017). Chapter 9 follows chapter 4 of Talbot (2024) and provides the iterative methods needed when no formula exists. Its last section lists the open questions of the research project that these notes prepare for.
The chapters were written as Jupyter notebooks, and the text calls them “notebook 1”, “notebook 2” and so on: notebook \(n\) is chapter \(n\).
Each chapter has the same shape:

What you will take away, in a few lines;
the ideas, each stated in plain words before any formula, each checked numerically as soon as it is stated;
real data from our telescope;
Your turn: exercises. Predict the answer before you run the cell;
Where to read more.

Do the chapters in order. Each uses what the previous ones built.

Running the code
Every chapter is a Jupyter notebook; this book is those notebooks, rendered with their outputs. To run and modify them:
cd notebooks/hno
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/jupyter lab
The few functions shared by the chapters live in hnotools.py, listed in the appendix. It is short on purpose: read it. The data are in data/m16_sample.npz, about 4.5 MB, described at the top of make_sample.py.

title: 1  The image deblurring problem
text:
1.1 A sharp image, a PSF, a blurred image
Companion notebook to Hansen, Nagy & O’Leary, Deblurring Images: Matrices, Spectra, and Filtering (SIAM, 2006), chapter 1. Read the chapter first; this notebook lets you run the ideas in Python, and ends on our own telescope data. The one-dimensional example is taken from H. Talbot’s lecture notes on optimisation.
What you will take away
Notation. The book writes \(x\) for the sharp image, \(b\) for the blurred one, \(e\) for the noise and \(A\) for the blurring matrix. Our project notes write \(y = k * x + n\): same thing, with \(b \leftrightarrow y\), \(e \leftrightarrow n\), and \(A\) = “convolve with the PSF \(k\)”. Capital letters (\(X\), \(B\), \(K\)) are Fourier transforms.
Our “true sky” \(x\) is a piece of the Pillars of Creation seen by the Hubble Space Telescope (oxygen filter). We blur it ourselves, so that for once we know the answer and can measure how well each method recovers it.
The point-spread function (PSF) is the image of a single point of light: what one star becomes after the atmosphere and the telescope. Blurring replaces every point of the sky by a copy of the PSF.
data = hno.load_sample()
x = data['hubble'].astype(float)                 # the true image, 256 x 256
psf = hno.gaussian_psf(x.shape, fwhm=6.0)        # a Gaussian blur, 6 pixels wide

noise_level = 0.005                              # 0.5 % of the brightest pixel
e = noise_level * rng.standard_normal(x.shape)
b_exact = hno.blur(x, psf)                       # A x
b = b_exact + e                                  # what a camera records

hno.show([x, psf[108:149, 108:149], b_exact, b],
         ['true image $x$', 'PSF (zoom)', 'blurred $A x$', 'blurred + noise $b$']);







Figure 1.1: The experiment of this chapter: a true image, the PSF, the blurred image, and the blurred image with noise.
The noise is barely visible. Keep that in mind: it is about to ruin everything.

title: 1  The image deblurring problem
text:
1.2 Blurring is linear
“Linear” means two things: blurring a sum gives the sum of the blurs, and blurring twice as bright an image gives twice as bright a result. Check it:

x1, x2 = x, np.roll(x, 40, axis=1)               # two different images
lhs = hno.blur(x1 + 2 * x2, psf)
rhs = hno.blur(x1, psf) + 2 * hno.blur(x2, psf)
print('largest difference:', np.abs(lhs - rhs).max())

largest difference: 1.7763568394002505e-15


Zero, up to rounding. So if we stack the pixels of an image into one long vector, blurring is a matrix product \(b = A x\).
How big is \(A\)? Our image has \(256 \times 256 = 65\,536\) pixels, so \(A\) is \(65\,536 \times 65\,536\):

n = x.size
print(f'A has {n**2:.2e} entries = {n**2 * 8 / 1e9:.0f} GB in double precision')

A has 4.29e+09 entries = 34 GB in double precision


We will never build \(A\). We do not need to: when the PSF is the same everywhere in the image and the boundaries are periodic, the convolution theorem says that blurring is a plain multiplication in Fourier space,
\[B(\nu) = K(\nu)\, X(\nu),\]
where \(K\), the Fourier transform of the PSF, is called the optical transfer function. In other words \(A\) is diagonal in the Fourier basis, and the values of \(K\) are its eigenvalues. This is all hno.blur does: open hnotools.py and read its three lines.
Chapters 3 and 4 of the book explain when this is exactly true and what to do at the image boundaries. For now, accept periodic boundaries.

title: 1  The image deblurring problem
section: 1.3 Seeing the matrix once: a one-dimensional signal
text:
1.3 Seeing the matrix once: a one-dimensional signal
Before inverting anything, let us look at a blurring matrix. For an image it is too big; for a one-dimensional signal it is not. The example below comes from H. Talbot’s Lecture Notes on Optimisation (chapter 2): a signal of 250 samples with steps and slow waves, blurred by a Gaussian kernel 25 samples long, with a tiny amount of noise.

N = 250
s = np.linspace(0, 3 * np.pi, N)
signal = 1.0 * (np.cos(2 * s) > 0) + 2 * np.sin(s / 4) + 0.1 * np.cos(3 * s + 1)

half = 12                                            # the kernel covers 2*12 + 1 = 25 samples
offsets = np.arange(-half, half + 1)
kernel = np.exp(-offsets**2 / (2 * 4.0**2))
kernel /= kernel.sum()

# Row i of A holds the kernel centred on sample i: one shifted copy per row.
A1 = sum(w * np.eye(N, k=o) for o, w in zip(offsets, kernel))
observed = A1 @ signal + 2e-4 * rng.standard_normal(N)
naive = np.linalg.solve(A1, observed)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.0), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1, 1.5, 1.5]})
ax[0].imshow(A1[:60, :60], cmap='gray_r'); ax[0].grid(False)
ax[0].set_title('top-left corner of $A$', loc='left'); ax[0].set_xticks([]); ax[0].set_yticks([])
ax[1].plot(s, signal, color=hno.INK2, lw=1.2, label='true signal')
ax[1].plot(s, observed, color=hno.BLUE, label='blurred + noise')
ax[1].set_title('the data', loc='left'); ax[1].legend(loc='lower right', fontsize=8)
ax[2].plot(s, naive, color=hno.ORANGE, lw=0.8)
ax[2].set_title('naive solution of $A x = b$', loc='left')
fig.tight_layout()
print(f'condition number of A: {np.linalg.cond(A1):.1e}')
print(f'largest value of the true signal: {np.abs(signal).max():.1f}   of the naive solution: {np.abs(naive).max():.1e}')

condition number of A: 1.1e+08
largest value of the true signal: 3.1   of the naive solution: 2.9e+03








Figure 1.2: A one-dimensional blur: the band structure of its matrix, the data, and the naive solution of the linear system.





Three things to notice.

\(A\) is a band: each row is the same kernel, shifted by one sample. All the structure of a blurring matrix is in that sentence, and chapter 4 of the book exploits it.
The condition number of \(A\) measures how much solving \(A x = b\) can amplify a relative error in \(b\). Here it is \(10^{8}\): an error of one part in ten thousand in the data may become an error ten thousand times larger than the signal.
And it does. The noise we added is invisible on the middle plot, about one part in ten thousand. The naive solution is wrong by three orders of magnitude.

The same thing will now happen with images. We cannot build their \(A\), but the convolution theorem gives us its eigenvalues for free.

title: 1  The image deblurring problem
text:
1.4 The naive solution
If \(B = K X\), then surely \(X = B / K\). First with no noise at all:

K = hno.psf2otf(psf)
x_naive_exact = np.real(ifft2(fft2(b_exact) / K))
print('relative error, noise-free data:', hno.rel_error(x_naive_exact, x))

relative error, noise-free data: 20.753292470784793


A relative error of 1 would mean “as wrong as a black image”. We are far beyond that, without any noise: the only errors in b_exact are rounding errors in the sixteenth digit. Now with the camera noise:

x_naive = np.real(ifft2(fft2(b) / K))
print('relative error, noisy data:', hno.rel_error(x_naive, x))
hno.show([x, b, x_naive], ['true image $x$', 'data $b$', 'naive solution $B/K$']);

relative error, noisy data: 650076042681940.1








Figure 1.3: The naive solution of the image problem.





The naive solution is pure garbage. Not “a bit noisy”: garbage.

title: 1  The image deblurring problem
text:
1.5 Why: look at the spectrum
Write the noisy data in Fourier space, \(B = K X + E\), and divide by \(K\):
\[\frac{B}{K} \;=\; X \;+\; \frac{E}{K}.\]
The first term is what we want. The second is the inverted noise. Noise has roughly the same strength at all frequencies, but \(K\) falls towards zero at high frequencies, because a blur erases fine detail. Dividing a constant by something tiny gives something enormous.
Figure 1.4 shows the three actors, averaged over all directions:

nu, K_r = hno.radial_profile(K)
_, X_r = hno.radial_profile(fft2(x))
_, E_r = hno.radial_profile(fft2(e))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
ax.semilogy(nu, X_r * K_r, color=hno.BLUE, label='blurred signal $|K X|$')
ax.semilogy(nu, E_r, color=hno.ORANGE, label='noise $|E|$')
ax.semilogy(nu, K_r, color=hno.INK2, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label='transfer function $|K|$')
ax.set_ylim(1e-18, 1e5); ax.set_xlim(0, 0.5)
ax.set_xlabel('spatial frequency (cycles / pixel)')
ax.set_title('Signal, noise and transfer function', loc='left')
ax.legend(loc='lower left');







Figure 1.4: Blurred signal, noise and transfer function against spatial frequency, averaged over all directions.





Read it from left to right.

At low frequencies the blurred signal is far above the noise: the data tell us about \(X\) there.
The two curves cross at about 0.13 cycles per pixel. Beyond that point the data are only noise: the signal that was there has been pushed below it.
\(|K|\) keeps falling, to \(10^{-14}\) at the right edge of the plot and lower still in the corners of the spectrum. There it meets the rounding floor of the computer, which is why even the noise-free inversion failed.

Dividing by \(K\) multiplies the noise by \(10^{5}\) at frequency 0.3 and by \(10^{11}\) at frequency 0.45. No measurement is good enough to survive that. The information is gone, and no algorithm can bring it back. What an algorithm can do is refrain from pretending.

title: 1  The image deblurring problem
section: 1.6 A first cure: do not divide where \(K\) is small
text:
1.6 A first cure: do not divide where \(K\) is small
The simplest honest method: invert where \(|K|\) is larger than a threshold \(\tau\), and put zero elsewhere.

def truncated_inverse(b, K, tau):
    """Invert only the frequencies where |K| > tau; zero the others."""
    keep = np.abs(K) > tau
    X = np.zeros_like(K)
    X[keep] = fft2(b)[keep] / K[keep]
    return np.real(ifft2(X))

taus = np.logspace(-4, -0.1, 40)
errors = [hno.rel_error(truncated_inverse(b, K, t), x) for t in taus]
best = taus[int(np.argmin(errors))]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.2))
ax.loglog(taus, errors, color=hno.BLUE)
ax.axhline(hno.rel_error(b, x), color=hno.INK2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 2)))
ax.text(taus[0], hno.rel_error(b, x) * 1.08, 'error of the blurred data itself', color=hno.INK2, fontsize=8)
ax.plot(best, min(errors), 'o', color=hno.ORANGE)
ax.set_xlabel(r'threshold $\tau$'); ax.set_ylabel('relative error')
ax.set_title('Too small: noise wins.  Too large: blur stays.', loc='left');
print(f'best threshold {best:.3f}: error {min(errors):.3f}  (blurred data: {hno.rel_error(b, x):.3f})')

best threshold 0.100: error 0.028  (blurred data: 0.041)








Figure 1.5: Relative error of the truncated inverse against the threshold. The dashed line is the error of the blurred data.





The U-shaped curve of Figure 1.5 is the single most important picture of the subject.

Left side (\(\tau\) too small): we invert frequencies that contain only noise, and the error explodes.
Right side (\(\tau\) too large): we throw away frequencies that did contain signal, and the result stays blurred.
In between there is a best compromise, and it is clearly better than doing nothing.


hno.show([b, truncated_inverse(b, K, best), x],
         ['data $b$', f'truncated inverse, $\\tau$ = {best:.3f}', 'true image $x$'], same_scale=True);







Figure 1.6: The data, the best truncated inverse, and the true image.





Sharper than the data, and no garbage. You can also see ripples, most clearly in the dark regions: cutting the spectrum abruptly creates them. Chapter 6 replaces the brutal cut by smoother filters (Tikhonov is the famous one), and chapter 5 explains the U-curve with the singular value decomposition.
One problem remains, and it is a serious one: we found the best \(\tau\) by comparing with the true image. With real data there is no true image.

title: 1  The image deblurring problem
section: 1.7 The real thing: one exposure of our telescope
text:
1.7 The real thing: one exposure of our telescope
Here is a single 5-minute exposure of the same region, taken with a 14 cm refractor, and its PSF. We did not choose this PSF: it was measured on the stars of that very exposure, which are natural point sources. It is not a Gaussian but a Moffat profile, with wider wings.

y = data['subs'][1].astype(float)                        # an exposure in median seeing
fmaj, fmin, pa, beta = data['sub_psf'][1]
k = hno.moffat_psf(y.shape, fmaj, fmin, pa, beta)
Ky = hno.psf2otf(k)
scale = float(data['pixel_scale'])
print(f'PSF width {np.sqrt(fmaj * fmin) * scale:.2f} arcsec  ({np.sqrt(fmaj * fmin):.2f} pixels),  Moffat beta {beta:.2f}')

hno.show([y, np.real(ifft2(fft2(y) / Ky)), truncated_inverse(y, Ky, 0.3), truncated_inverse(y, Ky, 0.05)],
         ['one exposure $y$', 'naive inverse', r'truncated, $\tau$ = 0.3', r'truncated, $\tau$ = 0.05'],
         same_scale=True);

PSF width 2.89 arcsec  (3.78 pixels),  Moffat beta 3.06








Figure 1.7: One real exposure, its naive inverse, and two truncated inverses.





Three things to see, all of them true of real data in general.

The naive inverse is garbage, as before.
With a threshold, the garbage is gone but the whole image is covered with rings centred on the two brightest stars. Cutting the spectrum abruptly is the same as convolving the image with an oscillating kernel, and the brighter the source, the stronger the oscillation: a star hundreds of times brighter than the nebula buries it. Worse, these two stars are saturated: the camera clipped them, so they do not obey \(y = k * x + n\) at all. A model violation is punished much harder than noise.
A bolder threshold adds amplified noise on top of the rings. And this time there is no U-curve to tell us where to stop, because nobody knows the true sky.

Three remarks that lead to the rest of the series and to our project.

A single exposure is mostly noise. That is why astronomers take hundreds and combine them. Notebook 8 shows that combining and deblurring are one and the same linear operation, if you do it right.
Choosing the amount of regularisation without the truth is the practical heart of the matter. Chapter 6 gives general-purpose rules. Our project uses a different idea: we declare in advance the resolution we will deliver, and then verify it on the stars of the result.
Stars and nebula want different treatments. In the project we measure the PSF on the stars, then remove them before deblurring the nebula.

title: 2  Images as arrays
text:
2.1 An image is an array
Companion notebook to Hansen, Nagy & O’Leary, Deblurring Images, chapter 2. The chapter shows how to handle images in MATLAB. This notebook covers the same ground with NumPy, and you can read it instead of the chapter.
What you will take away
Our working image is the average of 45 five-minute exposures of the Pillars of Creation through an oxygen filter, taken with a 14 cm refractor.
img = data['mean'].astype(float)
print('type :', type(img).__name__)
print('shape:', img.shape, ' (rows, columns)')
print('dtype:', img.dtype)
print(f'values from {img.min():.4f} to {img.max():.4f}, median {np.median(img):.5f}')

type : ndarray
shape: (256, 256)  (rows, columns)
dtype: float64
values from -0.0003 to 0.6288, median 0.00075
Three conventions to fix in your mind, because every bug in image code comes from one of them.
Cropping is slicing:
crop = img[131:191, 138:198]                 # 60 rows, 60 columns around a bright star
row, col = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(crop), crop.shape)
print('crop shape:', crop.shape, '  brightest pixel at row', row, 'column', col, 'of the crop')
hno.show([img, crop], ['the whole image', 'img[131:191, 138:198]'], width=3.4);

crop shape: (60, 60)   brightest pixel at row 21 column 12 of the crop








Figure 2.1: The mean of 45 exposures, and a crop obtained by slicing.
A slice is a view, not a copy: modifying crop would modify img. Write img[131:191, 138:198].copy() when you want an independent array.

title: 2  Images as arrays
text:
Index order is [row, column], that is [y, x], not [x, y].
Row 0 is at the top when displayed, as in a matrix, not at the bottom as on a graph.
Slices are half-open: img[100:160] takes rows 100 to 159.

title: 2  Images as arrays
section: 2.2 What you see is not what you have
text:
2.2 What you see is not what you have
hno.show made the nebula visible. Here is the same array displayed honestly, black for the smallest value and white for the largest:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1, 1.5]})
ax[0].imshow(img, vmin=img.min(), vmax=img.max()); ax[0].grid(False)
ax[0].set_xticks([]); ax[0].set_yticks([]); ax[0].set_title('linear display, min to max')
ax[1].hist(img.ravel(), bins=200, color=hno.BLUE, log=True)
ax[1].set_xlabel('pixel value'); ax[1].set_ylabel('number of pixels')
ax[1].set_title('histogram of the pixel values', loc='left')
fig.tight_layout()
p1, p99 = np.percentile(img, [1, 99])
print(f'99 % of the pixels lie between {p1:.4f} and {p99:.4f}: {(p99 - p1) / (img.max() - img.min()):.1%} of the full range')

99 % of the pixels lie between -0.0001 and 0.0029: 0.5% of the full range








Figure 2.2: The same image displayed linearly from its minimum to its maximum, and the histogram of its values.





Two stars and nothing else. The nebula is all there, but it occupies less than one percent of the range of values, squeezed against zero. Astronomical images have an enormous dynamic range, and a screen does not.
To look at such an image we stretch it: we choose which values become black and white, and how the values in between are spread. Three common choices:

def stretch(a, lo, hi, kind='linear'):
    """Map values lo..hi to 0..1 for display. Returns a NEW array."""
    z = np.clip((a - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1)
    if kind == 'sqrt':
        z = np.sqrt(z)
    elif kind == 'asinh':
        z = np.arcsinh(30 * z) / np.arcsinh(30)
    return z

lo, hi = np.percentile(img, [1, 99.9])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.6))
for a, kind in zip(ax, ('linear', 'sqrt', 'asinh')):
    a.imshow(stretch(img, lo, hi, kind), vmin=0, vmax=1); a.grid(False)
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.set_title(f'percentiles 1 to 99.9, {kind}')
fig.tight_layout()







Figure 2.3: Three stretches of the same array.





The three panels show the same array. None is more “true” than the others. The stretch is a choice made for the eye, and it should never leak into the numbers.

Why it matters: measure a star on stretched data and you are wrong
The width of a star image, its full width at half maximum (FWHM), is the standard measure of sharpness. Let us measure it on a synthetic star whose width we know, before and after a square-root stretch.

def fwhm_by_area(a):
    """FWHM of a single round blob: diameter of the disc of pixels above half maximum."""
    return 2 * np.sqrt(np.sum(a >= 0.5 * a.max()) / np.pi)

star = hno.moffat_psf((513, 513), 40.0, beta=2.5)       # a wide star, so that pixels are small
print(f'true FWHM            : 40.0')
print(f'measured, linear data: {fwhm_by_area(star):.1f}')
print(f'measured, sqrt data  : {fwhm_by_area(np.sqrt(star)):.1f}')

true FWHM            : 40.0
measured, linear data: 40.0
measured, sqrt data  : 60.9


Fifty percent too wide. The half maximum of the stretched star is not the half maximum of the star. An early version of our own study compared two telescopes on stretched images and got widths wrong by a factor of two; the mistake was found only when the measurement was redone on linear data.
Rule: stretch for the eye, compute on the linear data.

title: 2  Images as arrays
text:
2.3 Data types: integers lie
Image files usually store integers: 8 bits (0 to 255) for ordinary pictures, 16 bits (0 to 65 535) for cameras. NumPy keeps that type when it reads them, and integer arithmetic wraps around without warning:

a = np.array([200, 100, 50], dtype=np.uint8)
b = np.array([100, 100, 100], dtype=np.uint8)
print('a + b =', a + b, '   (200 + 100 should be 300)')
print('a - b =', a - b, '   (50 - 100 should be -50)')
print('as floats:', a.astype(float) + b, a.astype(float) - b)

a + b = [ 44 200 150]    (200 + 100 should be 300)
a - b = [100   0 206]    (50 - 100 should be -50)
as floats: [300. 200. 150.] [100.   0. -50.]


No error, no warning, wrong numbers. Convert to floating point as soon as you have read an image: img = img.astype(float).
The second danger of integers is quantisation. Let us save our image as an 8-bit PNG, as one would for a web page, and read it back.

tmp = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), 'nebula.png')
plt.imsave(tmp, img, cmap='gray', vmin=img.min(), vmax=img.max())     # linear, 8 bits
back = plt.imread(tmp)[:, :, 0].astype(float)                         # values k/255
back = back * (img.max() - img.min()) + img.min()                     # same units as img

levels = (p99 - p1) / (img.max() - img.min()) * 255
print(f'the nebula (99 % of the pixels) spans {levels:.1f} grey levels out of 255')
hno.show([img, back], ['original, floating point', 'after an 8-bit round trip'], width=3.6);

the nebula (99 % of the pixels) spans 1.2 grey levels out of 255








Figure 2.4: The image before and after being saved as an 8-bit file.





The whole nebula had to fit in about one grey level, and it is gone. This is why astronomers store images as 16-bit or floating-point FITS files, never as PNG or JPEG. (In Python, FITS files are read with the astropy package; our sample is stored as a NumPy .npz archive to keep the setup small.)

title: 2  Images as arrays
text:
2.4 Arithmetic on images
With floating-point arrays, image arithmetic is array arithmetic. Three examples that we will use again and again.
Averaging exposures. data['cube'] holds all 45 exposures of the central part of the field, as an array of shape (45, 128, 128).

cube = data['cube'].astype(float)
one = cube[0]
mean45 = cube.mean(axis=0)                   # average along the first axis: over the exposures
hno.show([one, mean45], ['one exposure', 'mean of 45'], same_scale=True, width=3.4);







Figure 2.5: One exposure and the mean of 45, on the same display scale.





Measuring noise by differencing. The sky does not change between two exposures, so their difference contains no sky: only noise. If each exposure has noise \(\sigma\), the difference has noise \(\sigma\sqrt{2}\).
The same trick measures the noise of the average: split the exposures in two halves, average each, and take half the difference of the two averages.
We estimate the spread with the median absolute deviation (MAD) rather than the standard deviation, because stars are not noise and a few bright pixels would dominate a standard deviation.

def robust_sigma(a):
    """Standard deviation estimated from the median absolute deviation."""
    return 1.4826 * np.median(np.abs(a - np.median(a)))

sigma_one = robust_sigma(cube[0] - cube[1]) / np.sqrt(2)
sigma_mean = robust_sigma(cube[0::2].mean(axis=0) - cube[1::2].mean(axis=0)) / 2
print(f'noise of one exposure : {sigma_one:.2e}')
print(f'noise of the mean     : {sigma_mean:.2e}')
print(f'ratio                 : {sigma_one / sigma_mean:.1f}    (sqrt(45) = {np.sqrt(45):.1f})')

noise of one exposure : 2.69e-04
noise of the mean     : 4.01e-05
ratio                 : 6.7    (sqrt(45) = 6.7)


Averaging \(N\) exposures divides the noise by about \(\sqrt{N}\). This is the whole reason for taking many exposures, and this “split in two halves” test is how our project puts error bars on its results.
Masks. A comparison gives an array of booleans, which selects pixels.

saturated = one > 0.5 * one.max()            # the camera clipped these pixels
print('saturated pixels in this exposure:', saturated.sum())
print(f'median of the sky, stars excluded: {np.median(one[~saturated]):.2e}')

saturated pixels in this exposure: 5
median of the sky, stars excluded: 9.12e-04

2.5 Colour images
A colour image is three images stacked along a third axis: shape (rows, columns, 3), in the order red, green, blue.
Our telescope camera is monochrome. We photograph the nebula three times through narrow filters that isolate the light of sulphur (S II), hydrogen (H\(\alpha\)) and oxygen (O III), and assign them to red, green and blue. This is the “Hubble palette” of the famous picture.

sho = data['mean_sho'].astype(float)         # shape (3, 256, 256): S II, H-alpha, O III
print('stored as', sho.shape)

rgb = np.stack([stretch(c, *np.percentile(c, [1, 99.8]), 'asinh') for c in sho], axis=-1)
print('for display', rgb.shape, ' values', rgb.min(), 'to', rgb.max())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12, 3.3))
for a, c, name in zip(ax, sho, ('S II  (red)', 'Hα  (green)', 'O III  (blue)')):
    a.imshow(stretch(c, *np.percentile(c, [1, 99.8]), 'asinh'), vmin=0, vmax=1); a.set_title(name)
ax[3].imshow(rgb); ax[3].set_title('colour composite')
for a in ax:
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()

stored as (3, 256, 256)
for display (256, 256, 3)  values 0.0 to 1.0








Figure 2.6: The three narrowband channels and their colour composite.





imshow expects a colour array of floats between 0 and 1, which is why each channel was stretched separately before stacking. The result is green almost everywhere, because hydrogen is by far the brightest gas in this nebula. Published pictures rebalance the three channels to taste: the colours are a display choice too. Chapter 7 comes back to colour, where each channel has its own blur.

text:
3.1 The PSF is the image of a point
Companion notebook to Hansen, Nagy & O’Leary, Deblurring Images, chapter 3.
What you will take away
Blur an image that is black except for one bright pixel. What comes out is, by definition, the PSF, centred where the pixel was.
point = np.zeros((64, 64)); point[20, 40] = 1.0
psf_small = hno.gaussian_psf((15, 15), fwhm=5.0)           # a 15 x 15 array holding the PSF

blurred_point = ndimage.convolve(point, psf_small, mode='constant')
two_points = point.copy(); two_points[45, 15] = 0.5
blurred_two = ndimage.convolve(two_points, psf_small, mode='constant')

hno.show([point, blurred_point, two_points, blurred_two],
         ['one point', 'its image: the PSF', 'two points', 'two PSFs, added'], lo=0, hi=100, gamma=1);







Figure 3.1: A point and its image; two points and their image.
Because blurring is linear, the image of any scene is the sum of the PSFs of all its points, each weighted by the brightness of the point. That operation has a name: convolution, written \(b = k * x\).
Two properties of a physical PSF that we will rely on:
print('minimum of the PSF:', psf_small.min(), '   sum of the PSF:', psf_small.sum())
print('total light before:', two_points.sum(), '   after:', round(blurred_two.sum(), 12))

minimum of the PSF: 6.729172487219203e-07    sum of the PSF: 1.0000000000000002
total light before: 1.5    after: 1.5

title: 3  The blurring function
text:
3.2 The matrix behind the convolution
Notebook 1 showed the matrix of a 1-D blur. Let us build the matrix of a 2-D blur, on an image small enough to afford it: \(12 \times 12\) pixels, hence \(A\) of size \(144 \times 144\).
To write \(b = A x\) the image must become a vector. Here the book and NumPy differ. MATLAB stacks the columns of the image; NumPy’s ravel() stacks the rows. Both are fine as long as you are consistent. We use NumPy’s order.
Column \(j\) of \(A\) is what \(A\) does to the \(j\)-th unit vector, that is, to an image with a single bright pixel. So column \(j\) is the PSF centred on pixel \(j\), flattened.

n = 12
psf_tiny = hno.gaussian_psf((7, 7), fwhm=3.0)

def build_matrix(n, psf, mode):
    """Blurring matrix of an n x n image, one column per pixel."""
    A = np.zeros((n * n, n * n))
    for j in range(n * n):
        unit = np.zeros(n * n); unit[j] = 1.0
        A[:, j] = ndimage.convolve(unit.reshape(n, n), psf, mode=mode).ravel()
    return A

A = build_matrix(n, psf_tiny, 'constant')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.6))
ax[0].imshow(A, cmap='gray_r'); ax[0].set_title('the matrix $A$ (144 x 144)')
ax[1].imshow(A[:36, :36], cmap='gray_r'); ax[1].set_title('its top-left corner')
ax[2].imshow(A[:, 5 * n + 6].reshape(n, n), cmap='gray'); ax[2].set_title('column 66, reshaped: a PSF')
for a in ax:
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()

x_test = rng.random((n, n))
print('A x equals the convolution:', np.allclose(A @ x_test.ravel(), ndimage.convolve(x_test, psf_tiny, mode='constant').ravel()))

A x equals the convolution: True








Figure 3.2: The blurring matrix of a 12 x 12 image, a detail of it, and one of its columns reshaped as an image.





\(A\) is made of blocks, each block is a band: bands inside bands. This regular structure is why we will never need to store \(A\); notebook 4 turns it into fast algorithms.

title: 3  The blurring function
section: 3.3 Where PSFs come from: three models
text:
3.3 Where PSFs come from: three models

Out-of-focus blur: a point becomes a uniform disc.
Gaussian blur: a convenient mathematical model, and a fair one for the sum of many small independent blurs.
Moffat blur: the shape of a star seen through the turbulent atmosphere with a long exposure. It has a Gaussian-like core and much wider wings, \(\;k(r) \propto \bigl(1 + r^2/\alpha^2\bigr)^{-\beta}\). This is the PSF of our telescope images.

The three PSFs below have the same full width at half maximum, 8 pixels.

shape = (129, 129)
yy, xx = np.indices(shape) - 64
disc = (np.hypot(xx, yy) <= 4.0).astype(float); disc /= disc.sum()
gauss = hno.gaussian_psf(shape, 8.0)
moffat = hno.moffat_psf(shape, 8.0, beta=2.5)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.3))
r = np.arange(0, 40)
for psf, name, col in ((disc, 'disc (defocus)', hno.AQUA), (gauss, 'Gaussian', hno.BLUE), (moffat, 'Moffat', hno.ORANGE)):
    ax[0].semilogy(r, psf[64, 64:64 + 40] / psf[64, 64], color=col, label=name)
    nu, otf = hno.radial_profile(hno.psf2otf(psf))
    ax[1].semilogy(nu, otf, color=col, label=name)
ax[0].set_ylim(1e-6, 2); ax[0].set_xlabel('distance from the centre (pixels)')
ax[0].set_title('the PSF, cut through its centre', loc='left'); ax[0].legend()
ax[1].set_ylim(1e-8, 2); ax[1].set_xlabel('spatial frequency (cycles / pixel)')
ax[1].set_title('its transfer function $|K|$', loc='left')
fig.tight_layout()







Figure 3.3: Three PSF models of the same width: a cut through the PSF (left) and the transfer function (right).





Same width, three very different inverse problems. Read the right-hand plot of Figure 3.3 with Figure 1.4 in mind: wherever \(|K|\) is small, the data hold no usable information.

The Gaussian kills high frequencies fastest: the hardest to invert.
The Moffat keeps a little of everything: its wide wings in image space are the price of a transfer function that decays slowly.
The disc has a transfer function that oscillates and dips to zero at regular intervals: some frequencies are erased exactly. (The dips do not quite reach zero on the plot because a disc drawn on a pixel grid is not perfectly round.)

title: 3  The blurring function
section: 3.4 Measuring the PSF on the data
text:
3.4 Measuring the PSF on the data
Models are useful, measurements are better. A star is so far away that it is a perfect point source, so each star in an image is a picture of the PSF, with some noise. Let us find stars in one of our exposures, cut one out, and fit a Moffat profile to it.

frame = data['subs'][1].astype(float)                     # an exposure in median seeing
stars = hno.find_stars(frame, n=8)
for row, col, peak in stars:
    print(f'star at row {row:3d}, column {col:3d}, peak {peak:.3f}')

star at row  72, column 233, peak 0.548
star at row 152, column 150, peak 0.336
star at row 161, column 169, peak 0.010
star at row  98, column 217, peak 0.006
star at row  86, column 217, peak 0.005
star at row 124, column 216, peak 0.004
star at row 202, column 223, peak 0.004
star at row 210, column  88, peak 0.003


The two brightest are saturated: the camera reached its maximum and clipped them, so they no longer show the true shape of the PSF. We take the brightest star that is safely below saturation.

row, col, peak = next(s for s in stars if s[2] < 0.25 * stars[0][2])
h = 10
stamp = frame[row - h:row + h + 1, col - h:col + h + 1]

def moffat_model(p, yy, xx):
    """Circular Moffat on a constant background. p = amplitude, y0, x0, alpha, beta, background."""
    amp, y0, x0, alpha, beta, bg = p
    return bg + amp * (1 + ((yy - y0)**2 + (xx - x0)**2) / alpha**2) ** (-beta)

yy, xx = np.indices(stamp.shape) - h
fit = optimize.least_squares(lambda p: (moffat_model(p, yy, xx) - stamp).ravel(),
                             x0=[stamp.max(), 0, 0, 3.0, 2.5, np.median(stamp)],
                             bounds=([0, -3, -3, 0.5, 1.1, -1], [10, 3, 3, 30, 10, 1]))
amp, y0, x0, alpha, beta, bg = fit.x
fwhm_fit = 2 * alpha * np.sqrt(2 ** (1 / beta) - 1)

fmaj, fmin, pa, beta_ref = data['sub_psf'][1]
print(f'our fit on one star   : FWHM {fwhm_fit:.2f} px, beta {beta:.2f}')
print(f'the project, 60 stars : FWHM {np.sqrt(fmaj * fmin):.2f} px, beta {beta_ref:.2f}')

model = moffat_model(fit.x, yy, xx)
dist = np.hypot(yy - y0, xx - x0).ravel()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12, 3.0), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1, 1, 1, 1.5]})
for a, im, name in zip(ax, (stamp, model, bg + 3 * (stamp - model)), ('the star', 'the Moffat fit', 'star minus fit (x 3)')):
    a.imshow(im, vmin=bg - 0.3 * amp, vmax=bg + amp); a.set_title(name)
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.grid(False)
ax[3].plot(dist, stamp.ravel() - bg, '.', color=hno.INK2, ms=3, label='pixels of the star')
rr = np.linspace(0, dist.max(), 200)
ax[3].plot(rr, amp * (1 + rr**2 / alpha**2) ** (-beta), color=hno.ORANGE, label='Moffat fit')
ax[3].set_xlabel('distance from the centre (pixels)'); ax[3].set_title('radial profile', loc='left'); ax[3].legend()
fig.tight_layout()

our fit on one star   : FWHM 3.65 px, beta 3.15
the project, 60 stars : FWHM 3.78 px, beta 3.06








Figure 3.4: A star of a real exposure, the Moffat profile fitted to it, the residual, and the radial profile.





One star, twenty lines of code, and we recover the width that the project measures by fitting sixty stars per exposure with an elliptical model. The remaining difference is honest: one faint star is a noisy estimate, and a round model cannot follow a slightly elongated PSF. The exponent \(\beta\) is the hardest parameter to pin down, because it is set by the faint wings.
This is the foundation of our project: the blur is not assumed, it is measured, exposure by exposure.

title: 3  The blurring function
text:
3.5 Noise
The noise in an astronomical image has two main sources.

Photon noise. Light arrives as photons, at random. If a pixel expects \(\lambda\) photons, it receives a Poisson-distributed number, with mean \(\lambda\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{\lambda}\). Brighter means noisier in absolute terms, but cleaner in relative terms.
Read noise. The electronics add a small Gaussian error to every pixel, the same everywhere.


levels = np.array([4, 25, 100, 400, 2500])
counts = rng.poisson(levels, size=(20000, len(levels)))
for lam, c in zip(levels, counts.T):
    print(f'expected {lam:5d} photons: measured mean {c.mean():7.1f}, std {c.std():5.1f}  (sqrt = {np.sqrt(lam):5.1f}),  relative noise {c.std() / lam:5.1%}')

expected     4 photons: measured mean     4.0, std   2.0  (sqrt =   2.0),  relative noise 50.3%
expected    25 photons: measured mean    25.0, std   5.0  (sqrt =   5.0),  relative noise 19.9%
expected   100 photons: measured mean   100.0, std  10.0  (sqrt =  10.0),  relative noise 10.0%
expected   400 photons: measured mean   399.9, std  20.0  (sqrt =  20.0),  relative noise  5.0%
expected  2500 photons: measured mean  2500.2, std  50.2  (sqrt =  50.0),  relative noise  2.0%


For our images there is a simplification. Through a narrow filter the nebula is faint, and most photons come from the sky background, which is the same everywhere. So the noise has nearly the same standard deviation in every pixel, and since it is the sum of many photons it is very nearly Gaussian. Check it on real data, using the difference of two exposures (notebook 2):

cube = data['cube'].astype(float)
diff = (cube[0] - cube[1]) / np.sqrt(2)
sigma = 1.4826 * np.median(np.abs(diff - np.median(diff)))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.2))
ax.hist(diff.ravel() / sigma, bins=np.linspace(-6, 6, 97), density=True, color=hno.BLUE, alpha=0.55, label='difference of two exposures')
t = np.linspace(-6, 6, 300)
ax.plot(t, np.exp(-t**2 / 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi), color=hno.ORANGE, label='Gaussian')
ax.set_yscale('log'); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1); ax.set_xlabel('value / $\\sigma$')
ax.set_title('Is the noise Gaussian?', loc='left'); ax.legend(loc='lower center');







Figure 3.5: Histogram of the difference of two exposures, in units of its standard deviation, with a Gaussian.





Gaussian over several orders of magnitude in the centre, with heavier tails: those are the stars, which are not identical in the two exposures because the blur changed. Keep this picture in mind for the rest of the series. “White Gaussian noise” is an excellent model of the sky and a poor model of bright stars.

title: 3  The blurring function
text:
3.6 Boundary conditions
A blurred pixel near the edge of a picture received light from points outside the picture. To write \(b = A x\) for the picture alone, we must say what the scene looks like out there. Three classical assumptions:

zero: the scene is black outside;
periodic: the scene repeats itself like a tiling;
reflexive: the scene outside is the mirror image of the scene inside.

None of them is true. To see how wrong each one is, we blur a large image (the truth), keep only its central part, and compare with what each assumption predicts from the central part alone.

big = data['hubble'].astype(float)                         # 256 x 256: the "whole scene"
psf_bc = hno.gaussian_psf((33, 33), fwhm=8.0)
inner = slice(64, 192)                                     # the camera sees the central 128 x 128

truth = ndimage.convolve(big, psf_bc, mode='reflect')[inner, inner]     # light from outside included
x_in = big[inner, inner]
panels, names = [], []
for mode, name in (('constant', 'zero'), ('wrap', 'periodic'), ('reflect', 'reflexive')):
    predicted = ndimage.convolve(x_in, psf_bc, mode=mode)
    err = np.abs(predicted - truth)
    panels.append(err); names.append(f'{name}: largest error {err.max():.3f}')
    print(f'{name:10s} error at the border {err[0, :].mean():.4f}   in the centre {err[48:80, 48:80].mean():.1e}')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.7))
for a, e, name in zip(ax, panels, names):
    a.imshow(e, vmin=0, vmax=0.15, cmap='gray_r'); a.set_title(name)
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()

zero       error at the border 0.1576   in the centre 0.0e+00
periodic   error at the border 0.1818   in the centre 0.0e+00
reflexive  error at the border 0.0041   in the centre 0.0e+00








Figure 3.6: Error of the three boundary conditions: white where the assumption is right, dark where it is wrong.





The error maps are white where the assumption is right and dark where it is wrong. All three are exact in the centre and wrong in a frame as wide as the PSF. The zero and periodic conditions are badly wrong here: the sky is never black, and the left edge of this scene does not resemble its right edge. The reflexive condition is forty times better, because a mirror image at least continues the scene without a jump.
An error in the model of the blur is not like noise: it is structured, and the inversion amplifies it just as eagerly. Deblurring with a wrong boundary condition produces ripples that start at the edges and travel inwards. Notebook 4 shows how each boundary condition leads to its own fast algorithm, and what to do in practice.

title: 4  Structured computations
text:
4.1 One dimension: three boundary conditions, three structures
Companion notebook to Hansen, Nagy & O’Leary, Deblurring Images, chapter 4.
The blurring matrix of a megapixel image has \(10^{12}\) entries. This notebook is about never building it.
What you will take away
Take a signal of 12 samples and a kernel of 5. The matrix of the blur depends on what we assume beyond the two ends.
N = 12
kern = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0]); kern /= kern.sum()

def matrix_1d(kern, N, mode):
    """Blurring matrix of a signal of length N: one column per sample."""
    return np.column_stack([ndimage.convolve1d(np.eye(N)[j], kern, mode=mode) for j in range(N)])

T = matrix_1d(kern, N, 'constant')       # zero boundary
C = matrix_1d(kern, N, 'wrap')           # periodic boundary
R = matrix_1d(kern, N, 'reflect')        # reflexive boundary

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.5))
for a, M, name in zip(ax, (T, C, R), ('zero: Toeplitz', 'periodic: circulant', 'reflexive: Toeplitz + Hankel')):
    a.imshow(M, cmap='gray_r', vmin=0, vmax=0.5); a.set_title(name)
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()







Figure 4.1: The blurring matrix of a one-dimensional signal under three boundary conditions.
In two dimensions the same three structures appear block-wise; the book names them BCCB, BTTB and so on. The names matter less than what each structure buys.

title: 4  Structured computations
text:
Zero boundary. The same values along every diagonal: a Toeplitz matrix. Light that falls off the ends is lost.
Periodic boundary. What leaves on one side comes back on the other: the diagonals wrap around the corners. Every row is the previous one shifted by one step, cyclically. This is a circulant matrix.
Reflexive boundary. What would leave is folded back: the corners gain entries along the anti-diagonals. Constant anti-diagonals define a Hankel matrix, so this one is Toeplitz plus Hankel.

title: 4  Structured computations
text:
4.2 Periodic boundaries: the FFT diagonalises \(A\)
Fact: every circulant matrix has the same eigenvectors, the complex sinusoids of the discrete Fourier transform. Its eigenvalues are the Fourier transform of its first column. Check both statements on \(C\):

eigvals_fft = fft(C[:, 0])
eigvals_num = np.linalg.eigvals(C)
print('eigenvalues from the FFT of the first column :', np.sort(eigvals_fft.real).round(4)[:6], '...')
print('eigenvalues from a general-purpose routine   :', np.sort(eigvals_num.real).round(4)[:6], '...')

x = rng.random(N)
print('C x  equals  ifft( fft(c) * fft(x) ):', np.allclose(C @ x, ifft(eigvals_fft * fft(x)).real))

eigenvalues from the FFT of the first column : [0.     0.     0.0595 0.0595 0.1111 0.1111] ...
eigenvalues from a general-purpose routine   : [-0.      0.      0.0595  0.0595  0.1111  0.1111] ...
C x  equals  ifft( fft(c) * fft(x) ): True


So multiplying by \(C\) costs two FFTs instead of a matrix product, and solving \(C x = b\) costs the same: divide by the eigenvalues instead of multiplying.
In two dimensions nothing changes except that fft becomes fft2. The first column of \(A\), reshaped as an image, is the PSF with its centre moved to pixel (0, 0) and wrapped around the corners. Verify on an \(8 \times 8\) image, where we can still afford the \(64 \times 64\) matrix:

n = 8
psf = hno.gaussian_psf((5, 5), fwhm=2.5)

def matrix_2d(n, psf, mode):
    A = np.zeros((n * n, n * n))
    for j in range(n * n):
        unit = np.zeros(n * n); unit[j] = 1.0
        A[:, j] = ndimage.convolve(unit.reshape(n, n), psf, mode=mode).ravel()
    return A

A_per = matrix_2d(n, psf, 'wrap')
first_column = A_per[:, 0].reshape(n, n)             # PSF centred on pixel (0, 0), wrapped
K = fft2(first_column)                               # the n*n eigenvalues, as an n x n array

X = rng.random((n, n))
print('A x equals ifft2(K * fft2(X)):', np.allclose((A_per @ X.ravel()).reshape(n, n), ifft2(K * fft2(X)).real))
print('eigenvalues agree            :', np.allclose(np.sort(np.linalg.eigvals(A_per).real), np.sort(K.real.ravel())))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8.4, 2.9))
for a, im, name in zip(ax, (psf, first_column, np.abs(K)), ('the PSF', 'first column of $A$', 'eigenvalues $|K|$')):
    a.imshow(im); a.set_title(name); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()

A x equals ifft2(K * fft2(X)): True
eigenvalues agree            : True








Figure 4.2: The PSF, the first column of the periodic blurring matrix, and its eigenvalues.





This is precisely what hno.psf2otf computes, and what notebook 1 used without proof. The array \(K\) has a name in optics: the optical transfer function.

title: 4  Structured computations
text:
4.3 Reflexive boundaries: the DCT diagonalises \(A\)
Notebook 3 showed that the reflexive boundary condition is the least wrong of the three. It has its own fast transform, on one condition: the PSF must be symmetric in both directions (left-right and up-down). Then \(A\) is diagonalised by the two-dimensional discrete cosine transform, the real-valued cousin of the FFT.
The eigenvalues are obtained from the first column of \(A\) again, with one extra division: if \(e_1\) is the image with a single 1 in the top-left corner,
\[S = \frac{\mathrm{dct2}(A\, e_1)}{\mathrm{dct2}(e_1)} .\]

A_ref = matrix_2d(n, psf, 'reflect')
e1 = np.zeros((n, n)); e1[0, 0] = 1.0
dct2 = lambda a: dctn(a, type=2, norm='ortho')
idct2 = lambda a: idctn(a, type=2, norm='ortho')

S = dct2(ndimage.convolve(e1, psf, mode='reflect')) / dct2(e1)      # no matrix needed
print('A x equals idct2(S * dct2(X)):', np.allclose((A_ref @ X.ravel()).reshape(n, n), idct2(S * dct2(X))))
print('eigenvalues agree            :', np.allclose(np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(A_ref)), np.sort(S.ravel())))

A x equals idct2(S * dct2(X)): True
eigenvalues agree            : True


At full size, with no matrix anywhere: blur a \(256 \times 256\) image with reflexive boundaries, then undo the blur exactly by dividing in the DCT domain. (No noise here; this only checks the algebra.)

x_true = data['hubble'].astype(float)
psf9 = hno.gaussian_psf((9, 9), fwhm=3.0)
b = ndimage.convolve(x_true, psf9, mode='reflect')

e1 = np.zeros_like(x_true); e1[0, 0] = 1.0
S = dct2(ndimage.convolve(e1, psf9, mode='reflect')) / dct2(e1)
x_back = idct2(dct2(b) / S)
print(f'smallest eigenvalue {np.abs(S).min():.1e},  relative error of the recovered image {hno.rel_error(x_back, x_true):.1e}')

smallest eigenvalue 8.8e-07,  relative error of the recovered image 3.7e-11

title: 4  Structured computations
text:
4.4 Separable blurs: Kronecker products
A PSF is separable when it is the product of a vertical profile and a horizontal profile: \(P = c\, r^{\mathsf T}\), a rank-one array. Blurring then splits into two independent 1-D blurs, columns first, rows next:
\[B = A_c\, X\, A_r^{\mathsf T},\]
where \(A_c\) and \(A_r\) are small 1-D blurring matrices, of the size of the image side. In vector form this is a Kronecker product. With NumPy’s row-by-row flattening,
\[\mathrm{vec}(A_c X A_r^{\mathsf T}) = (A_c \otimes A_r)\,\mathrm{vec}(X).\]
(The book flattens column by column and therefore writes \(A_r \otimes A_c\). Same mathematics, different bookkeeping.)

c = np.array([1.0, 4.0, 6.0, 4.0, 1.0]); c /= c.sum()          # vertical profile
r = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0]); r /= r.sum()                    # horizontal profile
P = np.outer(c, r)                                             # a separable 5 x 3 PSF

Ac, Ar = matrix_1d(c, n, 'constant'), matrix_1d(r, n, 'constant')
A_sep = matrix_2d(n, P, 'constant')
print('A equals kron(Ac, Ar)      :', np.allclose(A_sep, np.kron(Ac, Ar)))
print('A x equals Ac X Ar^T       :', np.allclose((A_sep @ X.ravel()).reshape(n, n), Ac @ X @ Ar.T))
print('storage: A has', A_sep.size, 'entries; Ac and Ar together', Ac.size + Ar.size)

A equals kron(Ac, Ar)      : True
A x equals Ac X Ar^T       : True
storage: A has 4096 entries; Ac and Ar together 128


The gain is that everything about \(A\) follows from the two small matrices: its inverse, its singular value decomposition (notebook 5), and so its regularised solutions, for any boundary condition, at the cost of working on \(n \times n\) matrices instead of \(n^2 \times n^2\).
Is a given PSF separable? Compute its singular values: a separable PSF has exactly one that is not zero.

fmaj, fmin, pa, beta = data['sub_psf'][1]
candidates = {'Gaussian': hno.gaussian_psf((33, 33), 6.0),
              'Moffat (round)': hno.moffat_psf((33, 33), 6.0, beta=2.5),
              'our telescope': hno.moffat_psf((33, 33), fmaj, fmin, pa, beta)}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.2))
for (name, p), col in zip(candidates.items(), (hno.BLUE, hno.ORANGE, hno.AQUA)):
    sv = np.linalg.svd(p, compute_uv=False)
    ax.semilogy(np.arange(1, 13), sv[:12] / sv[0], 'o-', color=col, label=name, ms=4)
    print(f'{name:15s} second singular value / first = {sv[1] / sv[0]:.1e}')
ax.set_ylim(1e-18, 3); ax.set_xlabel('index'); ax.set_title('singular values of the PSF array', loc='left'); ax.legend();

Gaussian        second singular value / first = 3.9e-17
Moffat (round)  second singular value / first = 5.6e-02
our telescope   second singular value / first = 6.6e-02








Figure 4.3: Singular values of three PSF arrays. A separable PSF has a single non-zero singular value.





The Gaussian is separable to machine precision: that is a special property of the Gaussian, and one reason for its popularity. A Moffat PSF is not, and neither is the real PSF of our telescope, although one separable term already captures most of it. The book explains how to use the best rank-one approximation when the PSF is nearly separable.

title: 4  Structured computations
section: 4.6 Realistic test data, and what to do at the edges
text:
4.6 Realistic test data, and what to do at the edges
A warning before the experiments of the next notebooks. If you create test data by blurring an image with periodic boundaries and then deblur it assuming periodic boundaries, the edges are perfectly consistent and you will see no edge problem. Real pictures are not that kind. The honest recipe:

blur an image larger than the one you will work with;
cut out the central part, so that light really did come from outside;
add noise.


def make_test_problem(big, psf, noise, margin=64, seed=1):
    """Blur a large scene, keep its centre, add noise. Returns (x_true, b)."""
    inner = slice(margin, big.shape[0] - margin)
    blurred = ndimage.convolve(big, psf, mode='reflect')[inner, inner]
    return big[inner, inner], blurred + noise * np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(blurred.shape)

psf17 = hno.gaussian_psf((17, 17), fwhm=4.0)
x_in, b_in = make_test_problem(data['hubble'].astype(float), psf17, noise=0.002)

Now deblur this honest test problem three ways, each with the simple “truncated inverse” of notebook 1 (invert where the eigenvalue is larger than \(\tau\), zero elsewhere):

assuming periodic boundaries, with the FFT;
assuming reflexive boundaries, with the DCT;
assuming periodic boundaries, after tapering the data: fading the image smoothly towards its mean value near the edges, so that the left edge matches the right one. This is what our project’s code does.


def truncated(coeffs, eig, tau):
    out = np.zeros_like(coeffs)
    keep = np.abs(eig) > tau
    out[keep] = coeffs[keep] / eig[keep]
    return out

def taper(b, width):
    """Fade the image to its mean over `width` pixels along every edge."""
    ramp = np.ones(b.shape[0])
    ramp[:width] = 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(np.pi * np.arange(width) / width)
    ramp[-width:] = ramp[:width][::-1]
    return b.mean() + (b - b.mean()) * np.outer(ramp, ramp)

tau = 0.05
m = x_in.shape[0]
big_psf = np.zeros((m, m)); big_psf[m//2 - 8:m//2 + 9, m//2 - 8:m//2 + 9] = psf17
K = hno.psf2otf(big_psf)
e1 = np.zeros((m, m)); e1[0, 0] = 1.0
S = dct2(ndimage.convolve(e1, psf17, mode='reflect')) / dct2(e1)

x_per = ifft2(truncated(fft2(b_in), K, tau)).real
x_ref = idct2(truncated(dct2(b_in), S, tau))
x_tap = ifft2(truncated(fft2(taper(b_in, 16)), K, tau)).real

core = slice(24, m - 24)                                   # judge away from the edges
for name, xr in (('periodic', x_per), ('reflexive', x_ref), ('periodic + taper', x_tap)):
    print(f'{name:17s} relative error: whole image {hno.rel_error(xr, x_in):.3f},   centre only {hno.rel_error(xr[core, core], x_in[core, core]):.3f}')
print(f'{"blurred data":17s} relative error: whole image {hno.rel_error(b_in, x_in):.3f},   centre only {hno.rel_error(b_in[core, core], x_in[core, core]):.3f}')

hno.show([x_per, x_ref, x_tap, x_in], ['periodic', 'reflexive', 'periodic + taper', 'true image'], same_scale=False, width=2.9);

periodic          relative error: whole image 0.232,   centre only 0.091
reflexive         relative error: whole image 0.015,   centre only 0.011
periodic + taper  relative error: whole image 0.172,   centre only 0.010
blurred data      relative error: whole image 0.014,   centre only 0.014








Figure 4.4: An honest test problem deblurred under three treatments of the edges.





Read the numbers together with the pictures.

Periodic, untreated: ripples parallel to the edges invade the picture. They come from the jump between opposite edges, which the periodic model takes for a real feature of the scene and tries to “deblur”.
Reflexive: the ripples are gone, at no extra cost. This is the right choice whenever the PSF is symmetric in both directions.
Tapering sacrifices a frame around the picture and saves the centre. It works with any PSF.

Our telescope PSF is an ellipse tilted at an arbitrary angle. It is symmetric through its centre, but not left-right and up-down separately, so the DCT route is closed to us:

k = hno.moffat_psf((33, 33), fmaj, fmin, pa, beta)
print('symmetric through the centre :', np.allclose(k, k[::-1, ::-1]))
print('symmetric left-right         :', np.allclose(k, k[:, ::-1]))
print(f'axis ratio {fmin / fmaj:.2f}, tilted by {pa:.0f} degrees')

symmetric through the centre : True
symmetric left-right         : False
axis ratio 0.87, tilted by 45 degrees


That is why the project works with the FFT and tapered edges, on images much larger than the PSF so that the sacrificed frame is cheap.

title: 5  The SVD and spectral analysis
text:
5.1 The SVD of a blur
Companion notebook to Hansen, Nagy & O’Leary, Deblurring Images, chapter 5.
Notebook 1 showed that the naive solution fails. This one shows why, with the one tool that explains every linear inverse problem: the singular value decomposition (SVD).
What you will take away
We start in one dimension, with the signal of notebook 1 and a \(250 \times 250\) blurring matrix, because there everything can be computed and plotted. (The Gaussian kernel is the same as in notebook 1, except that we no longer cut it short at 25 samples; exercise 4 shows what the cut does.)
Any matrix can be written
\[A = U\,\Sigma\,V^{\mathsf T} = \sum_i \sigma_i\, u_i\, v_i^{\mathsf T},\]
with orthonormal right singular vectors \(v_i\) (patterns in the scene), orthonormal left singular vectors \(u_i\) (patterns in the data), and singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0\). Read it as a three-step machine: decompose the scene on the patterns \(v_i\), multiply the \(i\)-th coefficient by \(\sigma_i\), rebuild with the patterns \(u_i\).
N = 250
s, signal = hno.lecture_signal(N)
A = hno.blur_matrix_1d(hno.gaussian_kernel_1d(4.0, 40), N)

U, sv, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
print('A equals U diag(sv) Vt:', np.allclose(A, U @ np.diag(sv) @ Vt))
print(f'largest singular value {sv[0]:.3f}, smallest {sv[-1]:.1e}, ratio (condition number) {sv[0] / sv[-1]:.1e}')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1, 1.4]})
ax[0].semilogy(np.arange(1, N + 1), sv, color=hno.BLUE)
ax[0].set_xlabel('index $i$'); ax[0].set_title('singular values $\\sigma_i$', loc='left')
for i, col in zip((0, 4, 19, 79), (hno.INK2, hno.BLUE, hno.ORANGE, hno.AQUA)):
    ax[1].plot(s, Vt[i] + 0.25 * (3 - (0, 4, 19, 79).index(i)), color=col, lw=1.2)
    ax[1].text(s[-1] + 0.1, 0.25 * (3 - (0, 4, 19, 79).index(i)), f'$v_{{{i + 1}}}$', va='center')
ax[1].set_yticks([]); ax[1].set_xlim(0, s[-1] + 0.9)
ax[1].set_title('four right singular vectors (shifted vertically)', loc='left')
fig.tight_layout()

A equals U diag(sv) Vt: True
largest singular value 0.999, smallest 8.4e-18, ratio (condition number) 1.2e+17

Two facts, true for every blur:
Together they say: a blur transmits smooth patterns well and fine patterns badly. That is all a blur is.

section: 5.2 The naive solution, channel by channel
text:
5.2 The naive solution, channel by channel
Since \(U\) and \(V\) are orthogonal, the solution of \(A x = b\) is
\[x_{\text{naive}} = \sum_i \frac{u_i^{\mathsf T} b}{\sigma_i}\; v_i .\]
Each coefficient of the data, \(u_i^{\mathsf T} b\), is divided by the gain of its channel. With noisy data \(b = b_{\text{exact}} + e\), each coefficient is the sum of a signal part and a noise part. Plot both, and the singular values:

noise = 2e-4
b_exact = A @ signal
b = b_exact + noise * rng.standard_normal(N)

coef_exact = np.abs(U.T @ b_exact)
coef = np.abs(U.T @ b)
idx = np.arange(1, N + 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
ax.semilogy(idx, sv, color=hno.INK2, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label='singular values $\\sigma_i$')
ax.semilogy(idx, coef_exact, '.', color=hno.AQUA, ms=4, label='exact data $|u_i^T b_{exact}|$')
ax.semilogy(idx, coef, '.', color=hno.BLUE, ms=4, label='noisy data $|u_i^T b|$')
ax.semilogy(idx, coef / sv, '.', color=hno.ORANGE, ms=4, label='naive coefficients $|u_i^T b| / \\sigma_i$')
ax.axhline(noise, color=hno.INK2, lw=0.8)
ax.text(N, noise * 1.6, 'noise level', ha='right', fontsize=8, color=hno.INK2)
ax.set_ylim(1e-19, 1e14); ax.set_xlabel('index $i$')
ax.set_title('The Picard plot', loc='left'); ax.legend(loc='lower left', fontsize=8);







Figure 5.2: The Picard plot of the one-dimensional problem.





Figure 5.2 is the Picard plot. Take the time to read it.

Green, exact data. The coefficients fall faster than the singular values (dashed). This is the discrete Picard condition: it means the exact problem has a decent solution, because \(|u_i^{\mathsf T} b| / \sigma_i\) stays bounded.
Blue, noisy data. The coefficients follow the green ones at first, then level off at the noise level. From there on, they are noise: the signal that used to be there is far below.
Orange, what the naive solution uses. Fine on the left. On the right, noise divided by smaller and smaller \(\sigma_i\): the coefficients grow without limit. The naive solution is dominated by its last, meaningless terms.

The index where the blue points meet the noise floor is the number of channels through which the data tell us anything.

title: 5  The SVD and spectral analysis
text:
5.3 Spectral filtering
The cure is now obvious: keep the terms that carry information, damp or drop the others. Every method of chapter 6 has the form
\[x_{\text{filt}} = \sum_i \phi_i\, \frac{u_i^{\mathsf T} b}{\sigma_i}\; v_i ,\]
with filter factors \(\phi_i\) close to 1 for the good channels and close to 0 for the bad ones. The simplest choice keeps the first \(k\) terms and drops the rest: the truncated SVD (TSVD).

def tsvd(U, sv, Vt, b, k):
    """Truncated SVD solution: the first k terms of the naive sum."""
    return Vt[:k].T @ ((U[:, :k].T @ b) / sv[:k])

ks = np.arange(1, 140)
errors = [hno.rel_error(tsvd(U, sv, Vt, b, k), signal) for k in ks]
k_best = int(ks[np.argmin(errors)])
k_floor = int(np.argmax(coef < 3 * noise)) + 1              # first coefficient at the noise floor
print(f'best k = {k_best} (error {min(errors):.3f});   first coefficient within 3x of the noise floor: i = {k_floor}')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.3), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1, 1.5]})
ax[0].semilogy(ks, errors, color=hno.BLUE); ax[0].plot(k_best, min(errors), 'o', color=hno.ORANGE)
ax[0].set_xlabel('number of terms $k$'); ax[0].set_title('relative error of the TSVD solution', loc='left')
ax[1].plot(s, signal, color=hno.INK2, lw=1.0, label='true signal')
for k, col in ((8, hno.AQUA), (k_best, hno.BLUE), (k_best + 12, hno.ORANGE)):
    ax[1].plot(s, tsvd(U, sv, Vt, b, k), color=col, lw=1.3, label=f'$k$ = {k}')
ax[1].set_ylim(-0.5, 4.2); ax[1].set_title('three TSVD solutions', loc='left'); ax[1].legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=8, ncol=2)
fig.tight_layout()

best k = 71 (error 0.044);   first coefficient within 3x of the noise floor: i = 59








Figure 5.3: Error of the truncated SVD against the number of terms, and three solutions.





The U-curve of notebook 1 (Figure 1.5) again, now explained term by term.

Too few terms: only smooth patterns are allowed, and the steps of the signal are rounded off (regularisation error).
Too many: noise-dominated terms enter with huge weights (perturbation error).
The best \(k\) sits close to where the Picard plot said the data hit the noise floor. You can read a good regularisation off the Picard plot without knowing the true signal.

Note what even the best solution cannot do: the steps stay rounded, with small oscillations next to them. Sharp steps need the fine patterns, and the data no longer contain them.

text:
5.4 Two dimensions: the patterns are images
For an image, the singular vectors are images too. With a separable blur (notebook 4) they are products of the 1-D patterns: if \(A = A_c \otimes A_r\), its singular vectors are \(v^c_i \otimes v^r_j\) and its singular values \(\sigma^c_i\, \sigma^r_j\). Here are a few of these basis images, for a Gaussian blur on a \(32 \times 32\) image:

n = 32
A1 = hno.blur_matrix_1d(hno.gaussian_kernel_1d(1.5, 5), n)
U1, s1, V1t = np.linalg.svd(A1)

pairs = [(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 2), (4, 3), (9, 9), (20, 22)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, len(pairs), figsize=(12, 2.4))
for a, (i, j) in zip(ax, pairs):
    a.imshow(np.outer(V1t[i], V1t[j]), cmap='gray')
    a.set_title(f'$\\sigma$ = {s1[i] * s1[j]:.1e}', fontsize=9)
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()







Figure 5.4: Six basis images of a separable Gaussian blur, with their singular values.





Same story as in 1-D: large singular values go with smooth images, small ones with fine checkerboards.
With periodic boundaries we do not even need to compute an SVD. Notebook 4 showed that \(A\) is diagonalised by the Fourier transform: the patterns are the sinusoids of each spatial frequency, and the singular values are the moduli of the transfer function,
\[\sigma_i \;\longleftrightarrow\; |K(\nu)| .\]
So for images, “index \(i\)” becomes “spatial frequency \(\nu\)”, and the Picard plot becomes the spectrum plot of notebook 1 (Figure 1.4). Here it is again in Picard form, the \(65\,536\) frequencies sorted by decreasing \(|K|\):

x_true = data['hubble'].astype(float)
psf = hno.gaussian_psf(x_true.shape, fwhm=6.0)
K = hno.psf2otf(psf)
noise2 = 0.005
B_exact = fft2(hno.blur(x_true, psf))
B = B_exact + fft2(noise2 * rng.standard_normal(x_true.shape))

order = np.argsort(-np.abs(K).ravel())
def running_median(a, w=400):
    a = a[: len(a) // w * w].reshape(-1, w)
    return np.median(a, axis=1)

i_axis = running_median(np.arange(K.size, dtype=float))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.6))
ax.semilogy(i_axis, running_median(np.abs(K).ravel()[order]), color=hno.INK2, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label='$|K|$, sorted')
ax.semilogy(i_axis, running_median(np.abs(B_exact).ravel()[order]), color=hno.AQUA, label='exact data')
ax.semilogy(i_axis, running_median(np.abs(B).ravel()[order]), color=hno.BLUE, label='noisy data')
ax.set_ylim(1e-18, 1e4); ax.set_xlabel('index (frequencies sorted by decreasing $|K|$)')
ax.set_title('Picard plot of the image problem of notebook 1', loc='left'); ax.legend(loc='upper right');
usable = int(np.sum(running_median(np.abs(B).ravel()[order]) > 2 * np.median(np.abs(B).ravel()[order][-20000:])) * 400)
print(f'frequencies clearly above the noise floor: about {usable} of {K.size}  ({usable / K.size:.1%})')

frequencies clearly above the noise floor: about 2800 of 65536  (4.3%)








Figure 5.5: Picard plot of the image problem of chapter 1.





Out of 65 536 unknowns, the data determine a few thousand. Everything else in a deblurred image comes from the method, not from the data. This is the number to keep in mind when someone shows you a spectacularly sharp restoration.

title: 5  The SVD and spectral analysis
text:
5.5 Real data: what stacking buys
For real data there is no “exact” curve. But we can still draw the two things that matter: the spectrum of the image, and the spectrum of its noise, which we measure by differencing as in notebook 2. Where the first sinks into the second, the information ends.
We do this for one exposure of our telescope and for the average of all 45, on a corner of the field that contains nebula but no bright star. (A star is a point, so its spectrum is flat and would hide what we want to see.)

cube = data['cube'].astype(float)[:, 2:66, 2:66]            # a 64 x 64 star-free corner, 45 exposures
scale = float(data['pixel_scale'])

def taper(b, width=8):
    ramp = np.ones(b.shape[0])
    ramp[:width] = 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(np.pi * np.arange(width) / width)
    ramp[-width:] = ramp[:width][::-1]
    return b.mean() + (b - b.mean()) * np.outer(ramp, ramp)

cases = (('one exposure', cube[0], (cube[0] - cube[1]) / np.sqrt(2), hno.ORANGE),
         ('mean of 45 exposures', cube.mean(axis=0), (cube[0::2].mean(axis=0) - cube[1::2].mean(axis=0)) / 2, hno.BLUE))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
for name, img, noise_img, col in cases:
    nu, spec = hno.radial_profile(fft2(taper(img)))
    _, nspec = hno.radial_profile(fft2(taper(noise_img)))
    knee = nu[1 + np.argmax(spec[1:] < 2 * nspec[1:])]
    ax.semilogy(nu / scale, spec, color=col, label=name)
    ax.semilogy(nu / scale, nspec, color=col, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
    print(f'{name:22s} noise level {np.median(nspec[5:]):.2e},  image within 2x of its noise from {knee / scale:.2f} cycles/arcsec')
ax.plot([], [], color=hno.INK2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)), label='its noise (measured by differencing)')
ax.set_xlabel('spatial frequency (cycles / arcsecond)')
ax.set_title('Spectrum of real images, and of their noise', loc='left'); ax.legend();

one exposure           noise level 1.12e-02,  image within 2x of its noise from 0.10 cycles/arcsec
mean of 45 exposures   noise level 1.65e-03,  image within 2x of its noise from 0.20 cycles/arcsec








Figure 5.6: Spectrum of one exposure and of the mean of 45 (solid lines), and of their noise (dotted lines).





Averaging 45 exposures lowers the noise by a factor close to \(\sqrt{45} \approx 7\) and leaves the signal where it was. The point where the image sinks into its noise moves from about 0.10 to about 0.20 cycles per arcsecond. In two dimensions, twice the radius means four times as many channels carrying information, so four times as much of the scene that can honestly be restored. No deblurring algorithm can do this; only more photons can.
This is why our project never deblurs single exposures. Notebook 8 shows how to combine them so that not one of these newly usable channels is wasted.
