title: 6  Regularisation by spectral filtering
text:
6.1 Two filters
Companion notebook to Hansen, Nagy & O’Leary, Deblurring Images, chapter 6, with the optimisation point of view of H. Talbot’s Lecture Notes on Optimisation, chapter 3.
Notebook 5 ended on a formula: a regularised solution is a filtered sum, \(x_{\text{filt}} = \sum_i \phi_i\, (u_i^{\mathsf T} b / \sigma_i)\, v_i\). This notebook is about choosing the filter factors \(\phi_i\), and above all about choosing how much to filter when the true image is unknown.
What you will take away
Both leave the large singular values alone (\(\phi \approx 1\)) and suppress the small ones (\(\phi \approx 0\)). The parameter, \(\tau\) or \(\alpha\), is the singular value at which the filter switches.
sig = np.logspace(-6, 0, 400)
alpha = 1e-3
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.0))
ax.semilogx(sig, (sig > alpha).astype(float), color=hno.ORANGE, label='truncated SVD, $\\tau = 10^{-3}$')
ax.semilogx(sig, sig**2 / (sig**2 + alpha**2), color=hno.BLUE, label='Tikhonov, $\\alpha = 10^{-3}$')
ax.set_xlabel('singular value $\\sigma_i$'); ax.set_title('filter factors $\\phi_i$', loc='left'); ax.legend();







Figure 6.1: Filter factors of the truncated SVD and of Tikhonov regularisation.
Note the Tikhonov factor for a small singular value: \(\phi_i / \sigma_i
\approx \sigma_i / \alpha^2\), which goes to zero instead of infinity. The division by a tiny number has been replaced by a multiplication by a tiny number.

title: 6  Regularisation by spectral filtering
text:
Truncated SVD: keep the \(k\) largest singular values, drop the others. \(\phi_i = 1\) if \(\sigma_i > \tau\), else \(0\).
Tikhonov: damp smoothly, \(\;\phi_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{\sigma_i^2 + \alpha^2}\).

title: 6  Regularisation by spectral filtering
section: 6.2 Tikhonov regularisation is a least-squares problem
text:
6.2 Tikhonov regularisation is a least-squares problem
The lecture notes introduce Tikhonov regularisation from a different door. Instead of solving \(A x = b\), look for the \(x\) that explains the data and stays small:
\[x_\alpha = \arg\min_x \;\|A x - b\|_2^2 \;+\; \alpha^2 \|x\|_2^2 .\]
The first term asks for fidelity to the data, the second penalises the wild oscillations that the naive solution is made of, and \(\alpha\) sets the exchange rate between the two. Setting the gradient to zero gives a linear system, the regularised normal equations,
\[(A^{\mathsf T} A + \alpha^2 I)\, x = A^{\mathsf T} b ,\]
whose matrix is symmetric positive definite, hence always invertible.
Is this the same solution as the Tikhonov filter? Check on the 1-D problem of notebook 5, where we have both the matrix and its SVD.

N = 250
s, signal = hno.lecture_signal(N)
A = hno.blur_matrix_1d(hno.gaussian_kernel_1d(4.0, 40), N)
b = A @ signal + 2e-4 * rng.standard_normal(N)
U, sv, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)

alpha = 3e-3
x_filter = Vt.T @ (sv / (sv**2 + alpha**2) * (U.T @ b))                         # filtered SVD sum
x_normal = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + alpha**2 * np.eye(N), A.T @ b)             # normal equations
print('largest difference between the two solutions:', np.abs(x_filter - x_normal).max())
print(f'relative error of the Tikhonov solution: {hno.rel_error(x_filter, signal):.3f}')

largest difference between the two solutions: 2.196867132653324e-10
relative error of the Tikhonov solution: 0.044


Identical. Insert \(A = U \Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\) in the normal equations and the filter factors \(\sigma_i^2 / (\sigma_i^2 + \alpha^2)\) fall out in two lines (exercise 1).
The two views are worth keeping side by side.

The filter view is the one that computes fast, whenever a fast transform diagonalises \(A\).
The optimisation view is the one that generalises: change the penalty, add constraints, replace the square by a robust loss, and the minimisation problem still makes sense when no SVD can help. Notebooks 7 and 9 go down that road, and so does our project.

title: 6  Regularisation by spectral filtering
section: 6.3 Deblurring an image with both filters
text:
6.3 Deblurring an image with both filters
For images we use a fast transform. The Gaussian PSF is symmetric, so we take reflexive boundaries and the cosine transform (notebook 4); the eigenvalues \(S\) of the blur play the role of the singular values.
In this section and the next two, the test data are created with the same reflexive boundaries that the solver assumes. Notebook 4 called this the “inverse crime”, and it is one. We commit it on purpose: the rules of section 6.5 are derived for data that obey the model exactly, plus white noise, and we first want to see them work under their own assumptions. Section 6.5 ends with what happens when the assumptions fail.

from scipy import ndimage

psf = hno.gaussian_psf((25, 25), fwhm=6.0)
noise_level = 0.002
x_true = data['hubble'].astype(float)
b_img = ndimage.convolve(x_true, psf, mode='reflect') + noise_level * rng.standard_normal(x_true.shape)

S = hno.dct_eigenvalues(psf, b_img.shape)
B = hno.dct2(b_img)

def tsvd_image(B, S, tau):
    X = np.zeros_like(B); keep = np.abs(S) > tau
    X[keep] = B[keep] / S[keep]
    return hno.idct2(X)

def tikhonov_image(B, S, alpha):
    return hno.idct2(S * B / (S**2 + alpha**2))

params = np.logspace(-4, 0, 60)
err_tsvd = [hno.rel_error(tsvd_image(B, S, p), x_true) for p in params]
err_tikh = [hno.rel_error(tikhonov_image(B, S, p), x_true) for p in params]
tau_best, alpha_best = params[np.argmin(err_tsvd)], params[np.argmin(err_tikh)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.2))
ax.loglog(params, err_tsvd, color=hno.ORANGE, label='truncated SVD'); ax.loglog(params, err_tikh, color=hno.BLUE, label='Tikhonov')
ax.axhline(hno.rel_error(b_img, x_true), color=hno.INK2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 2)))
ax.text(params[0], hno.rel_error(b_img, x_true) * 1.07, 'blurred data', fontsize=8, color=hno.INK2)
ax.set_ylim(0.006, 1); ax.set_xlabel('parameter ($\\tau$ or $\\alpha$)'); ax.set_ylabel('relative error'); ax.legend()
ax.set_title('Error against the regularisation parameter', loc='left');
print(f'blurred data              error {hno.rel_error(b_img, x_true):.4f}')
print(f'truncated SVD, best tau   {tau_best:.3f}: error {min(err_tsvd):.4f}')
print(f'Tikhonov,      best alpha {alpha_best:.3f}: error {min(err_tikh):.4f}')

blurred data              error 0.0240
truncated SVD, best tau   0.070: error 0.0098
Tikhonov,      best alpha 0.060: error 0.0105








Figure 6.2: Relative error of the two filters against their parameter.






hno.show([b_img, tsvd_image(B, S, tau_best), tikhonov_image(B, S, alpha_best), x_true],
         ['blurred + noise', 'truncated SVD (best)', 'Tikhonov (best)', 'true image'], same_scale=True, width=2.9);







Figure 6.3: The data, the best result of each filter, and the true image.





Both filters do about equally well at their best setting, and both curves have the U shape. For too large a parameter Tikhonov loses sooner, because its filter starts damping well before \(\sigma_i = \alpha\). Its advantages lie elsewhere: no ripples from an abrupt cut, and a formulation as a minimisation problem, which is the one that generalises.

title: 6  Regularisation by spectral filtering
section: 6.4 Two errors that pull in opposite directions
text:
6.4 Two errors that pull in opposite directions
With \(b = A x + e\), the filtered solution differs from the truth by
\[x_{\text{filt}} - x \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_i (\phi_i - 1)\,(v_i^{\mathsf T} x)\, v_i}_{\text{regularisation error}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\sum_i \phi_i\, \frac{u_i^{\mathsf T} e}{\sigma_i}\, v_i}_{\text{perturbation error}} .\]

The regularisation error is the part of the true image that the filter removed. It grows with \(\alpha\).
The perturbation error is the noise that the filter let through, amplified. It shrinks with \(\alpha\).

In an experiment we know \(x\) and \(e\), so we can compute each part:

X_true = hno.dct2(x_true)
E = B - S * X_true                                   # the noise, in the transform domain
reg_err, pert_err = [], []
for a in params:
    phi = S**2 / (S**2 + a**2)
    reg_err.append(np.linalg.norm((phi - 1) * X_true) / np.linalg.norm(X_true))
    pert_err.append(np.linalg.norm(phi * E / S) / np.linalg.norm(X_true))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.2))
ax.loglog(params, reg_err, color=hno.AQUA, label='regularisation error')
ax.loglog(params, pert_err, color=hno.ORANGE, label='perturbation error')
ax.loglog(params, err_tikh, color=hno.BLUE, label='total error')
ax.set_ylim(1e-3, 10); ax.set_xlabel('$\\alpha$'); ax.legend(); ax.set_title('Tikhonov: the two parts of the error', loc='left');







Figure 6.4: Regularisation error, perturbation error, and their total, for Tikhonov regularisation.





In Figure 6.4 the best \(\alpha\) is close to where the two curves cross. Every parameter-choice rule below is an attempt to locate that crossing without seeing either curve.

title: 6  Regularisation by spectral filtering
text:
6.5 Choosing \(\alpha\) without knowing the truth
All three rules use only the data, through the residual \(r_\alpha = b - A x_\alpha\), whose coefficients in the transform domain are \((1 - \phi_i)\, \hat b_i\).
Discrepancy principle. If we knew the truth, the residual would be the noise, of squared norm about \(N \sigma^2\) for \(N\) pixels of noise \(\sigma\). So choose the \(\alpha\) whose residual has just that size: explain the data down to the noise, and no further. Needs the noise level.
Generalised cross-validation (GCV). A good \(x_\alpha\) should predict a data value that was left out. Averaged over all pixels this gives a function to minimise, \[G(\alpha) = \frac{\|r_\alpha\|^2}{\bigl(\sum_i (1 - \phi_i)\bigr)^2} .\] Needs nothing.
L-curve. Plot \(\log\|x_\alpha\|\) against \(\log\|r_\alpha\|\) for all \(\alpha\). The curve looks like an L; the corner is where reducing the residual further starts to cost a large increase in the solution. Needs nothing.

grid = np.logspace(-5, 0, 200)

def residual_norm(B, S, a):
    return np.linalg.norm(a**2 / (S**2 + a**2) * B)             # (1 - phi) * B

def solution_norm(B, S, a):
    return np.linalg.norm(S * B / (S**2 + a**2))

def gcv(B, S, a):
    one_minus_phi = a**2 / (S**2 + a**2)
    return np.sum((one_minus_phi * B)**2) / np.sum(one_minus_phi)**2

def choose_alpha(B, S, sigma):
    """The three rules. Returns a dict {rule: alpha}."""
    dp = 10 ** optimize.brentq(lambda la: residual_norm(B, S, 10**la) - np.sqrt(B.size) * sigma, -6, 1)
    g = grid[np.argmin([gcv(B, S, a) for a in grid])]
    rho = np.log([residual_norm(B, S, a) for a in grid]); eta = np.log([solution_norm(B, S, a) for a in grid])
    d1r, d1e = np.gradient(rho), np.gradient(eta)
    curvature = (d1r * np.gradient(d1e) - np.gradient(d1r) * d1e) / (d1r**2 + d1e**2) ** 1.5
    return {'discrepancy principle': dp, 'GCV': g, 'L-curve': grid[5 + np.argmax(curvature[5:-5])]}

def report(B, S, sigma, x_ref, b_ref):
    errs = [hno.rel_error(tikhonov_image(B, S, a), x_ref) for a in grid]
    rules = {'best possible (uses the truth)': grid[np.argmin(errs)], **choose_alpha(B, S, sigma)}
    print(f'{"rule":32s} {"alpha":>8s}   relative error      (blurred data: {hno.rel_error(b_ref, x_ref):.4f})')
    for name, a in rules.items():
        print(f'{name:32s} {a:8.4f}   {hno.rel_error(tikhonov_image(B, S, a), x_ref):.4f}')
    return rules

rules = report(B, S, noise_level, x_true, b_img)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.3))
ax[0].loglog(grid, [gcv(B, S, a) for a in grid], color=hno.BLUE); ax[0].axvline(rules['GCV'], color=hno.ORANGE, lw=1)
ax[0].set_xlabel('$\\alpha$'); ax[0].set_title('GCV function, and its minimum', loc='left')
ax[1].plot(np.log([residual_norm(B, S, a) for a in grid]), np.log([solution_norm(B, S, a) for a in grid]), color=hno.BLUE)
for (name, a), col in zip(list(rules.items())[1:], (hno.AQUA, hno.ORANGE, hno.INK2)):
    ax[1].plot(np.log(residual_norm(B, S, a)), np.log(solution_norm(B, S, a)), 'o', color=col, label=name)
ax[1].set_xlabel('log residual norm'); ax[1].set_ylabel('log solution norm'); ax[1].set_title('L-curve', loc='left'); ax[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout()

rule                                alpha   relative error      (blurred data: 0.0240)
best possible (uses the truth)     0.0622   0.0104
discrepancy principle              0.0353   0.0138
GCV                                0.0174   0.0264
L-curve                            0.0043   0.1035








Figure 6.5: The GCV function with its minimum, and the L-curve with the choices of the three rules.





Compare each rule with the first line, the only one that used the true image.

The discrepancy principle lands close to the best possible choice. It was told the noise level, and here the noise is exactly what it assumes.
GCV, which was told nothing, regularises too little, and its result is no better than the blurred data.
The L-curve corner is badly placed on this problem: it regularises far too little and the result is worse than the data. The L-curve is known to struggle when the true image is very smooth, which is our case.

None of the rules is infallible, and on another problem their ranking can change. This is the honest state of the art; the book discusses the strengths and failure modes of each.
Estimating the noise level. The discrepancy principle needs \(\sigma\). It can be read off the data: at the highest frequencies the blurred signal has vanished (notebook 5), so those coefficients are pure noise.

m = B.shape[0]
high = B[m // 2:, m // 2:]                                     # the high-frequency quarter
sigma_hat = 1.4826 * np.median(np.abs(high))
print(f'noise estimated from the data: {sigma_hat:.5f}     true value: {noise_level}')

noise estimated from the data: 0.00201     true value: 0.002



When the assumptions fail
Now the honest version of the same experiment (notebook 4): the scene is larger than the picture, so light really came from outside, and the reflexive boundary is only an approximation. Same PSF, same noise, same rules.

x_h, b_h = hno.make_test_problem(x_true, psf, noise=noise_level)
S_h, B_h = hno.dct_eigenvalues(psf, b_h.shape), hno.dct2(b_h)
report(B_h, S_h, noise_level, x_h, b_h);

rule                                alpha   relative error      (blurred data: 0.0238)
best possible (uses the truth)     0.0740   0.0164
discrepancy principle              0.0237   0.0291
GCV                                0.0104   0.0550
L-curve                            0.0034   0.1392


All three rules now regularise too little, and the “restored” images are worse than the blurred one. Nothing is wrong with the code. The residual \(b - A x_\alpha\) now contains two things: the noise, and the error of the model at the edges, which is not white noise at all. The rules cannot tell them apart. They see structure in the residual, conclude that the solution does not yet explain the data, and push \(\alpha\) down to chase an error that no \(x\) can explain.
This is the most practical lesson of the notebook: parameter-choice rules are only as good as the model of the data. With real images the model is never exact: the PSF is measured with some error, it varies across the field, bright stars saturate. The next section shows a rule that asks less of the model.

title: 6  Regularisation by spectral filtering
section: 6.6 Real data, and a fourth rule
text:
6.6 Real data, and a fourth rule
Let us deblur a real image: the average of our 45 exposures. First measure its PSF on a star (notebook 3), then apply Tikhonov regularisation with the parameter chosen by GCV. The PSF is not symmetric in general, so we use the FFT with tapered edges (notebook 4). With complex eigenvalues \(K\), the Tikhonov solution reads \(X = \bar K\, Y / (|K|^2 + \alpha^2)\).

y = data['mean'].astype(float)
star = hno.fit_star(y, 161, 169)                               # an unsaturated star
print(f'PSF of the mean image: FWHM {star["fwhm"]:.2f} px = {star["fwhm"] * float(data["pixel_scale"]):.2f} arcsec, Moffat beta {star["beta"]:.2f}')

K = hno.psf2otf(hno.moffat_psf(y.shape, star['fwhm'], beta=star['beta']))
Y = fft2(hno.taper(y))

def gcv_fft(a):
    one_minus_phi = a**2 / (np.abs(K)**2 + a**2)
    return np.sum(np.abs(one_minus_phi * Y)**2) / np.sum(one_minus_phi)**2

alpha_real = grid[np.argmin([gcv_fft(a) for a in grid])]
x_gcv = ifft2(np.conj(K) * Y / (np.abs(K)**2 + alpha_real**2)).real
print(f'GCV chooses alpha = {alpha_real:.4f};   star FWHM after deblurring: {hno.fit_star(x_gcv, 161, 169)["fwhm"]:.2f} px')

PSF of the mean image: FWHM 3.23 px = 2.46 arcsec, Moffat beta 2.72
GCV chooses alpha = 0.0018;   star FWHM after deblurring: 0.72 px


A star narrower than one pixel is not a restoration. GCV has chosen a tiny \(\alpha\), and the result is close to the naive inverse: this is the failure of the previous section, on real data, where the model is never exact (the PSF is itself a noisy measurement, and the bright stars are saturated).
There is a deeper problem. Even when a rule behaves, how sharp is the result supposed to be? Tikhonov regularisation does not say: the resolution of the output is whatever comes out, and it differs from image to image.
Our project turns the question around, following Magain et al. (1998). Decide first what PSF the result should have: a narrower one than the data, the target \(t\), but not infinitely narrow. Then aim at the sky seen through that target, \(t * x\), instead of the sky itself:
\[X_t = T\,\frac{\bar K\, Y}{|K|^2 + \lambda} .\]
It is the Tikhonov filter (with \(\lambda = \alpha^2\)) multiplied by the transfer function \(T\) of the target, which removes on purpose the highest frequencies, those we could never have restored. And the choice of \(\lambda\) becomes a contract: take the largest \(\lambda\), hence the least noise, for which a star of the result really has the declared width.

target_fwhm = 0.8 * star['fwhm']                               # declare: 20 % sharper than the data
T = hno.psf2otf(hno.gaussian_psf(y.shape, target_fwhm))

print(f'declared target: {target_fwhm:.2f} px')
chosen = None
for lam in (1e-1, 3e-2, 1e-2, 3e-3, 1e-3, 3e-4, 1e-4):
    x_t = ifft2(T * np.conj(K) * Y / (np.abs(K)**2 + lam)).real
    delivered = hno.fit_star(x_t, 161, 169)['fwhm']
    ok = delivered <= 1.05 * target_fwhm
    print(f'  lambda {lam:7.0e}: delivered {delivered:.2f} px  {"<- contract met" if ok and chosen is None else ""}')
    if ok and chosen is None:
        chosen = (lam, x_t)

crop = (slice(100, 228), slice(100, 228))
hno.show([y[crop], x_gcv[crop], chosen[1][crop]],
         ['mean of 45 exposures', f'Tikhonov, GCV', f'target {target_fwhm:.2f} px, $\\lambda$ = {chosen[0]:.0e}'], same_scale=True, width=3.4);

declared target: 2.58 px
  lambda   1e-01: delivered 4.24 px  
  lambda   3e-02: delivered 3.65 px  
  lambda   1e-02: delivered 3.27 px  
  lambda   3e-03: delivered 2.98 px  
  lambda   1e-03: delivered 2.82 px  
  lambda   3e-04: delivered 2.70 px  <- contract met
  lambda   1e-04: delivered 2.63 px  








Figure 6.6: The mean of 45 real exposures, its Tikhonov restoration with the GCV parameter, and its restoration to a declared target.





Look at the three images.

The GCV result is noise, as the sub-pixel star had warned.
The target version is a credible, slightly sharper image, and it states what it delivers: we checked it on a star. That check is the whole difference between a restoration and a measurement.
It also shows a dark ring around the saturated star: the model violation of notebook 1, still with us. The project removes the stars before deblurring the nebula for exactly this reason.

One limitation remains. The average of 45 exposures has one PSF, a blend of 45 different ones. The sharp exposures have been diluted by the blurred ones before we even started. Notebook 8 removes that limitation.

title: 7  Colour images and smoothing norms
text:
7.1 Colour: blurring across channels
Companion notebook to Hansen, Nagy & O’Leary, Deblurring Images, chapter 7, with the penalties of H. Talbot’s Lecture Notes on Optimisation, chapter 3.
Chapter 7 of the book opens three doors beyond the basic method. This notebook walks through each of them.
What you will take away
A colour image has three channels. Two kinds of blur can affect it.
If every channel has the same spatial blur, the full model is a Kronecker product, \((A_{\text{color}} \otimes A)\,x = b\): mixing and blurring act on different “axes” of the data and do not interfere.
scene = np.stack([c / np.percentile(c, 99.5) for c in data['mean_sho'].astype(float)])   # 3 x 256 x 256
A_color = np.array([[0.70, 0.20, 0.10],
                    [0.15, 0.70, 0.15],
                    [0.10, 0.20, 0.70]])                       # rows sum to 1: no light lost
psf = hno.gaussian_psf(scene.shape[1:], fwhm=3.0)

mix = lambda M, img: np.einsum('ij,jhw->ihw', M, img)          # apply a 3 x 3 matrix to the channels
blur3 = lambda img: np.stack([hno.blur(c, psf) for c in img])  # blur each channel

b1 = blur3(mix(A_color, scene))                                # mix, then blur
b2 = mix(A_color, blur3(scene))                                # blur, then mix
print('the two orders give the same image:', np.allclose(b1, b2))

unmixed = mix(np.linalg.inv(A_color), b1)                      # undo the mixing: a 3 x 3 inverse
print('after unmixing, each channel is just a blurred channel:', np.allclose(unmixed, blur3(scene)))
print(f'condition number of A_color: {np.linalg.cond(A_color):.1f}')

the two orders give the same image: True
after unmixing, each channel is just a blurred channel: True
condition number of A_color: 2.0
Because the two operations commute, the inverse problem splits: first undo the colour mixing, which is a well-conditioned \(3 \times 3\) system, then deblur each channel separately with everything we already know. The hard part is still the spatial blur.

text:
7.2 Our case: no mixing, but three different PSFs
Our colour images are made differently (notebook 2): three separate series of exposures through three narrow filters, on different nights. There is no cross-channel mixing, \(A_{\text{color}} = I\). But the atmosphere was not the same on each night, so each channel has its own PSF. Measure it on two unsaturated stars:

sho = data['mean_sho'].astype(float)
names = ('S II  (red)', 'Hα  (green)', 'O III  (blue)')
stars = ((161, 169), (98, 217))
psf_params = []
for name, c in zip(names, sho):
    fits = [hno.fit_star(c, r, col) for r, col in stars]
    fwhm, beta = np.mean([f['fwhm'] for f in fits]), np.mean([f['beta'] for f in fits])
    psf_params.append((fwhm, beta))
    print(f'{name:14s} FWHM {fwhm:.2f} px = {fwhm * float(data["pixel_scale"]):.2f} arcsec')

S II  (red)    FWHM 2.68 px = 2.04 arcsec
Hα  (green)    FWHM 2.73 px = 2.09 arcsec
O III  (blue)  FWHM 3.21 px = 2.45 arcsec


The oxygen channel is about 20 % blurrier than the other two. In a colour composite, every star is then a sharp red-green core inside a wider blue disc: a colour fringe. The radial profiles of a star in the three channels, each scaled to its peak, show it directly:

def star_profile(c, row=161, col=169, half=10):
    """Radial profile of a star, background removed, scaled to the fitted peak."""
    f = hno.fit_star(c, row, col)
    stamp = c[row - half:row + half + 1, col - half:col + half + 1]
    yy, xx = np.indices(stamp.shape) - half
    dist = np.hypot(yy - (f['row'] - row), xx - (f['col'] - col)).ravel()
    values = ((stamp - f['bg']) / f['amp']).ravel()
    edges = np.arange(0, 7.5, 1.0)
    return 0.5 * (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]), np.array([np.median(values[(dist >= a) & (dist < b)]) for a, b in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:])])

def plot_profiles(ax, channels, title):
    for c, name, colour in zip(channels, names, (hno.ORANGE, hno.AQUA, hno.BLUE)):
        r, prof = star_profile(c)
        ax.plot(r, prof, 'o-', color=colour, ms=4, label=name)
    ax.set_xlabel('distance from the centre of the star (pixels)'); ax.set_title(title, loc='left')

The remedy uses the target idea of notebook 6. Choose one target PSF for the three channels, and filter each channel with its own measured PSF \(K_c\):
\[X_c = T\,\frac{\bar K_c\, Y_c}{|K_c|^2 + \lambda} .\]
After this, all three channels show the sky through the same PSF \(T\). We declare the width of the sharpest channel as the common target.

target = min(f for f, _ in psf_params)
T = hno.psf2otf(hno.gaussian_psf(sho.shape[1:], target))
matched = []
for (fwhm, beta), c in zip(psf_params, sho):
    K = hno.psf2otf(hno.moffat_psf(c.shape, fwhm, beta=beta))
    matched.append(ifft2(T * np.conj(K) * fft2(hno.taper(c)) / (np.abs(K)**2 + 1e-3)).real)
matched = np.stack(matched)

print(f'declared common target: {target:.2f} px')
for name, c in zip(names, matched):
    print(f'{name:14s} delivered {np.mean([hno.fit_star(c, r, col)["fwhm"] for r, col in stars]):.2f} px')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2), sharey=True)
plot_profiles(ax[0], sho, 'before: three different PSFs'); ax[0].legend()
plot_profiles(ax[1], matched, 'after: one common target')
fig.tight_layout()

declared common target: 2.68 px
S II  (red)    delivered 2.75 px
Hα  (green)    delivered 2.79 px
O III  (blue)  delivered 2.87 px








Figure 7.1: Radial profile of a star in the three channels, before and after matching to a common target.





The three widths now agree to within 4 %, against 20 % before, and the profiles fall on top of each other: the fringe is gone. (The widths are a few percent above the target because of the regularisation \(\lambda\); notebook 6 showed how to trade that against noise.) For a scientist this matters far beyond looks: the ratio of two channels measures the physical state of the gas, and a ratio of two images taken through different PSFs is wrong near every sharp feature.
This “PSF matching to a declared target” is one of the things our project does to every image.

title: 7  Colour images and smoothing norms
text:
7.3 Tikhonov revisited: penalise the derivative
Notebook 6 penalised the size of the solution, \(\alpha^2\|x\|^2\). But why should a good image be small? A more sensible belief is that a good image is smooth: neighbouring pixels have similar values. The lecture notes write the general form
\[x_\alpha = \arg\min_x \;\|A x - b\|^2 + \alpha^2 \|L x\|^2 ,
\qquad (A^{\mathsf T} A + \alpha^2 L^{\mathsf T} L)\,x = A^{\mathsf T} b ,\]
with \(L\) the identity (small solution), the gradient (small variations) or the Laplacian (small curvature).
With a fast transform nothing changes but the filter. For reflexive boundaries, \(L^{\mathsf T} L\) is diagonalised by the same cosine transform as \(A\), and the filter factors become
\[\phi = \frac{S^2}{S^2 + \alpha^2\, \ell^2}, \qquad
\ell^2_{\text{gradient}}(k, l) = \bigl(2 - 2\cos\tfrac{\pi k}{n}\bigr) + \bigl(2 - 2\cos\tfrac{\pi l}{n}\bigr),
\qquad \ell^2_{\text{Laplacian}} = \bigl(\ell^2_{\text{gradient}}\bigr)^2 .\]
\(\ell^2\) is zero at frequency zero and grows with frequency: the penalty leaves the smooth part of the image alone and charges only for the fine detail, which is where the noise lives.

x_true = data['hubble'].astype(float)
psf25 = hno.gaussian_psf((25, 25), fwhm=6.0)
b_img = ndimage.convolve(x_true, psf25, mode='reflect') + 0.002 * rng.standard_normal(x_true.shape)
S, B = hno.dct_eigenvalues(psf25, b_img.shape), hno.dct2(b_img)

n = b_img.shape[0]
one_d = 2 - 2 * np.cos(np.pi * np.arange(n) / n)
grad2 = one_d[:, None] + one_d[None, :]
penalties = {'identity': np.ones_like(grad2), 'gradient': grad2, 'Laplacian': grad2**2}

alphas = np.logspace(-4, 1, 61)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.2))
best = {}
for (name, L2), col in zip(penalties.items(), (hno.INK2, hno.BLUE, hno.ORANGE)):
    errs = [hno.rel_error(hno.idct2(S * B / (S**2 + a**2 * L2 + 1e-300)), x_true) for a in alphas]
    best[name] = (alphas[np.argmin(errs)], min(errs))
    ax.loglog(alphas, errs, color=col, label=name)
    print(f'{name:10s} best alpha {best[name][0]:.3f}: relative error {best[name][1]:.4f}')
ax.set_ylim(0.006, 1); ax.set_xlabel('$\\alpha$'); ax.set_ylabel('relative error'); ax.legend()
ax.set_title('Three penalties on the image problem of notebook 6', loc='left');

identity   best alpha 0.068: relative error 0.0105
gradient   best alpha 0.100: relative error 0.0089
Laplacian  best alpha 0.121: relative error 0.0088








Figure 7.2: Relative error of three Tikhonov penalties against the regularisation parameter.





The derivative penalties do better than the identity, by about 15 % here, and the two of them are close to each other. A real gain, obtained for free, but not a revolution: all three are squared penalties, and they share a limitation that the next section makes visible.

text:
7.4 Other norms: keeping the edges
Back to the 1-D signal, which has sharp steps. Solve the three Tikhonov problems with explicit matrices, each at its best \(\alpha\):

N = 250
s, signal = hno.lecture_signal(N)
A = hno.blur_matrix_1d(hno.gaussian_kernel_1d(4.0, 40), N)
b = A @ signal + 2e-4 * rng.standard_normal(N)

D = np.diff(np.eye(N), axis=0)                                 # first differences: (N-1) x N
operators = {'identity': np.eye(N), 'gradient': D, 'Laplacian': np.diff(np.eye(N), 2, axis=0)}

def tikhonov_general(A, b, L, alpha):
    return np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + alpha**2 * L.T @ L, A.T @ b)

solutions = {}
for name, L in operators.items():
    err, a = min((hno.rel_error(tikhonov_general(A, b, L, a), signal), a) for a in np.logspace(-5, 1, 61))
    solutions[name] = tikhonov_general(A, b, L, a)
    print(f'{name:10s} best alpha {a:.4f}: relative error {err:.4f}')

identity   best alpha 0.0010: relative error 0.0419
gradient   best alpha 0.0010: relative error 0.0421
Laplacian  best alpha 0.0013: relative error 0.0422


Three penalties, the same error to within one percent. On this signal the choice of \(L\) changes nothing, because the error is entirely in the steps, and a squared penalty hates steps: one jump of height \(h\) costs \(h^2\), while the same rise spread over ten samples costs ten times \((h/10)^2\), that is ten times less. Squared penalties always prefer the ramp to the step.
The cure is to penalise the absolute value of the derivative instead of its square:
\[x = \arg\min_x \;\|A x - b\|^2 + \alpha \,\|D x\|_1 , \qquad \|D x\|_1 = \sum_i |x_{i+1} - x_i| .\]
Now a jump of height \(h\) costs \(h\) however it is spread: steps are no longer punished. This is total variation regularisation.
The price: the problem is not quadratic any more, so there is no linear system and no filter. We need an iterative algorithm. Here is one in a few lines, of the majorise-minimise family described in chapter 4 of the lecture notes: replace \(|t|\) by a quadratic that touches it at the current solution, solve that Tikhonov problem, repeat.

def total_variation(A, b, alpha, iterations=60, eps=1e-3):
    """Total-variation deblurring by majorise-minimise: a sequence of
    weighted Tikhonov problems. Notebook 9 explains why this works."""
    x = tikhonov_general(A, b, D, 1e-2)                         # any reasonable start
    for _ in range(iterations):
        w = 1.0 / np.sqrt((D @ x)**2 + eps**2)                  # large weight where the signal is flat
        x = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + alpha * D.T @ (w[:, None] * D), A.T @ b)
    return x

x_tv = total_variation(A, b, alpha=1e-3)
print(f'total variation: relative error {hno.rel_error(x_tv, signal):.4f}')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.3))
for a, (lo, hi) in zip(ax, ((0, N), (50, 120))):
    a.plot(s[lo:hi], signal[lo:hi], color=hno.INK2, lw=1.0, label='true signal')
    a.plot(s[lo:hi], solutions['gradient'][lo:hi], color=hno.ORANGE, lw=1.5, label='Tikhonov, gradient penalty')
    a.plot(s[lo:hi], x_tv[lo:hi], color=hno.BLUE, lw=1.5, label='total variation')
ax[0].set_title('the whole signal', loc='left'); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8)
ax[1].set_title('zoom on two steps', loc='left')
fig.tight_layout()

total variation: relative error 0.0215








Figure 7.3: Tikhonov regularisation with a gradient penalty, and total variation, on the one-dimensional signal.





Half the error, and the steps are steps again. The same data, the same blur, the same noise: only our belief about the unknown changed, from “smooth” to “piecewise smooth, with a few jumps”.
Two warnings before you fall in love with it.

The result is exactly as good as the belief. Total variation turns gentle slopes into small staircases, and would do damage to an image that really is smooth, such as a nebula.
We have left the world of filters. There are no filter factors to plot and no Picard plot to tell us what came from the data and what came from the penalty. That loss of transparency is the price of every powerful prior, and it is the reason our project insists on verifying its results.

text:
8.1 Forty-five exposures, forty-five PSFs
This notebook has no chapter in Hansen, Nagy & O’Leary. It applies everything the book taught to the situation of every astronomer: not one blurred image, but many, each with its own blur. It is the starting point of our research project. Reference: B. Zackay & E. Ofek, “How to COADD images. II”, The Astrophysical Journal 836, 188 (2017).
What you will take away
data['cube'] holds 45 exposures of five minutes each, taken on several nights. data['all_psf'] holds, for each one, the PSF measured on its stars (notebook 3), the small registration error left after aligning the exposures, and the noise level.

         [f'a sharp exposure ({fwhm[sharp]:.1f}")', f'a blurry one ({fwhm[blurry]:.1f}")', 'the mean of all 45'], same_scale=True);

The width of the PSF varies by more than a factor of two. The mean of all exposures (right) has little noise, but it is blurrier than the best exposures: averaging has diluted the sharp exposures in the blurry ones.

title: 8  From one frame to many: proper coaddition
text:
8.2 The model and its solution
Write the model of notebook 1 once per exposure. All exposures see the same sky \(x\); exposure \(i\) has its own PSF \(k_i\) and its own noise level \(s_i\):
\[y_i = k_i * x + n_i, \qquad n_i \sim \mathcal N(0, s_i^2 I), \qquad i = 1, \dots, N .\]
Least squares, each exposure weighted by its noise (a noisy exposure counts less):
\[\hat x = \arg\min_x \;\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{2 s_i^2}\,\|y_i - k_i * x\|^2 .\]
In Fourier space every convolution is a product, the sum of squares separates frequency by frequency, and each frequency is a one-unknown least-squares problem. Setting the derivative to zero gives
\[S(\nu)\,X(\nu) = R(\nu), \qquad
R = \sum_i \frac{\bar K_i\, Y_i}{s_i^2}, \qquad S = \sum_i \frac{|K_i|^2}{s_i^2} .\]
\(S\) goes to zero at high frequencies, as \(|K|^2\) did for one image, so we regularise exactly as in notebook 6: a declared target PSF \(t\) and a small \(\lambda\),
\[\hat X_t = T\,\frac{R}{S + \lambda\,S(0)} .\]
This is proper coaddition. With \(N = 1\) it is the target filter of notebook 6.
One detail before coding it. The exposures are aligned to a fraction of a pixel, not perfectly. A shift by \((d_x, d_y)\) multiplies the Fourier transform by a phase, \(e^{-2\pi i(\nu_x d_x + \nu_y d_y)}\) (the shift theorem), so the residual shift of each exposure simply goes into its \(K_i\).

def frame_otf(shape, p, zoom=1.0):
    """Transfer function K_i of one exposure: its Moffat PSF, shifted by its
    registration error. p = (fmaj, fmin, pa, beta, dx, dy, ...)."""
    K = hno.psf2otf(hno.moffat_psf(shape, p[0] * zoom, p[1] * zoom, p[2], p[3]))
    nu_y, nu_x = fftfreq(shape[0])[:, None], fftfreq(shape[1])[None, :]
    return K * np.exp(-2j * np.pi * (nu_x * p[4] * zoom + nu_y * p[5] * zoom))

def proper_coadd(Y, K, s, T, lam):
    """Y, K: arrays (N, h, w) of Fourier transforms and transfer functions;
    s: noise levels (N,); T: transfer function of the target; lam: regularisation."""
    w = (1.0 / s**2)[:, None, None]
    R = np.sum(w * np.conj(K) * Y, axis=0)
    S = np.sum(w * np.abs(K)**2, axis=0)
    return ifft2(T * R / (S + lam * S.flat[0])).real

def stack_then_deblur(Y, K_mean, T, lam):
    """The classical pipeline: average the exposures, then one target filter."""
    return ifft2(T * np.conj(K_mean) * Y.mean(axis=0) / (np.abs(K_mean)**2 + lam)).real

Two functions of three lines each. Everything else in this notebook is measurement.

8.3 A controlled experiment
First with a known truth. We take the Hubble image as the sky and simulate 45 exposures of it with the 45 real PSFs and the real relative noise levels of our data. (The Hubble image has pixels half the size of ours, so the PSF widths are doubled to keep the same sky scale.)
The three contenders, all aiming at the same target of 1.8 arcsec:

the plain mean, not deblurred;
the mean, then deblurred, using the exact PSF of the mean (a generous assumption: in real life it has to be fitted);
proper coaddition.


x = data['hubble'].astype(float)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

8.4 Where the gain comes from
Look at one spatial frequency \(\nu\). In the sum \(R\), exposure \(i\) enters with the weight \(\bar K_i / s_i^2\): it counts in proportion to how well it transmits that frequency. A blurry exposure has \(K_i(\nu) \approx 0\) at a high frequency and simply does not vote there; at low frequencies, where it is as good as any other, it votes fully.
Here is the share of each exposure in \(S\), at a low and at a high frequency:

shape = cube.shape[1:]
K_all = np.array([frame_otf(shape, p) for p in P])
weights = np.abs(K_all)**2 / noise[:, None, None]**2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.0))
for (iy, ix), name, col in (((0, 4), '0.04 cycles/arcsec (large structures)', hno.AQUA), ((0, 32), '0.33 cycles/arcsec (fine detail)', hno.ORANGE)):
    share = weights[:, iy, ix] / weights[:, iy, ix].sum()
    ax.plot(np.arange(1, N + 1), 100 * share[order], 'o-', color=col, ms=3.5, label=name)
ax.axhline(100 / N, color=hno.INK2, lw=0.8); ax.text(N, 100 / N * 1.15, 'equal shares', ha='right', fontsize=8, color=hno.INK2)
ax.set_xlabel('exposures, sorted from sharpest to blurriest'); ax.set_ylabel('share of the information (%)')
ax.set_title('Who is trusted, at two spatial frequencies', loc='left'); ax.legend();







Figure 8.4: Share of each exposure in the information, at a low and at a high spatial frequency.





Figure 8.4 tells the story. For the large structures every exposure contributes about equally: nothing is wasted. For the fine detail, a handful of sharp exposures carry almost everything and the blurry ones are ignored. Proper coaddition is lucky imaging decided frequency by frequency, without throwing a single photon away.
The size of the gain can be written down. At each frequency, the ratio of the squared signal-to-noise ratios of proper coaddition and of the plain mean is
\[G(\nu) = \frac{S(\nu)\,\sum_i s_i^2}{\bigl|\sum_i K_i(\nu)\bigr|^2} \;\ge\; 1 ,\]
by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, with equality only if all exposures have the same PSF and the same noise. Deblurring the mean afterwards cannot change its signal-to-noise ratio at any frequency (it multiplies signal and noise by the same number), so \(G\) is also the advantage over the classical pipeline. And \(G\) needs only the PSFs and the noise levels: it can be computed before any coaddition is done.

S_real = weights.sum(axis=0)
G = S_real * np.sum(noise**2) / np.abs(K_all.sum(axis=0))**2
nu, G_r = hno.radial_profile(G)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.0))
ax.semilogy(nu / scale, G_r, color=hno.BLUE)
ax.axhline(1, color=hno.INK2, lw=0.8)
ax.set_yticks([1, 2, 3, 5, 7]); ax.set_yticklabels(['1', '2', '3', '5', '7']); ax.minorticks_off()
ax.set_xlabel('spatial frequency (cycles / arcsecond)'); ax.set_title('Predicted gain $G$ for these 45 exposures', loc='left');
print(f'G at 0.3 cycles/arcsec: {G_r[np.argmin(np.abs(nu / scale - 0.3))]:.2f}')

G at 0.3 cycles/arcsec: 1.84








Figure 8.5: Predicted gain of proper coaddition over the plain mean, for the 45 real exposures.





Figure 8.5 predicts no gain for the large structures, a factor of almost two at 0.3 cycles per arcsecond, more beyond. For the two other colour channels of this nebula, whose exposures were taken in steadier conditions, the same computation gives 1.15: hardly any gain to expect. Whether this prediction matches the gain actually measured, across many fields and instruments, is the question of our research project.

8.5 The real exposures
Now the real cube. There is no true image, so we judge as in notebook 6: the width of a star in the result, and the noise, measured by processing the even and the odd exposures separately and taking half the difference (notebook 2).
For the classical pipeline we do what one does in practice: measure the PSF of the mean on a star, and deblur the mean with it.

Y_all = np.array([fft2(hno.taper(f, 12)) for f in cube])
T = hno.psf2otf(hno.gaussian_psf(shape, 2.36)).real                    # target: 2.36 px = 1.8 arcsec
star = (97, 105)                                                       # an unsaturated star
fit_mean = hno.fit_star(cube.mean(axis=0), *star)
K_of_mean = hno.psf2otf(hno.moffat_psf(shape, fit_mean['fwhm'], beta=fit_mean['beta']))

quiet = (slice(4, 44), slice(4, 44))                                   # a corner without bright stars

def measure(pipeline, lam):
    """Star width (arcsec) of the full result, and its noise from the even/odd split."""
    full = pipeline(np.arange(N), lam)

run_classic = lambda idx, lam: stack_then_deblur(Y_all[idx], K_of_mean, T, lam)

8.6 The weak point: every exposure is trusted
Least squares has no notion of a wrong measurement. Go back to the simulation and spoil one exposure out of 45 with a satellite trail, a bright line that the model knows nothing about.

bad = 10
yy, xx = np.indices(x.shape)
trail = 3.0 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((yy - 0.45 * xx - 60) / 1.5)**2)          # a bright oblique line
Y_bad = Y_sim.copy()
Y_bad[bad] = Y_sim[bad] + fft2(trail)

lam = lams[np.argmin(err_proper)]
clean = proper_coadd(Y_sim, K_sim, s_sim, T_sim, lam)
spoiled = proper_coadd(Y_bad, K_sim, s_sim, T_sim, lam)
print(f'error without the trail: {error(clean):.4f}     with one spoiled exposure: {error(spoiled):.4f}')
hno.show([ifft2(Y_bad[bad]).real, clean, spoiled], ['the spoiled exposure', 'coadd of 45 clean exposures', 'coadd with the spoiled one'], width=3.3);

error without the trail: 0.0228     with one spoiled exposure: 0.0425








Figure 8.7: One spoiled exposure, the coadd of the clean exposures, and the coadd that includes the spoiled one.





One exposure in forty-five, and the trail is in the final image, and the error has almost doubled. The classical average at least has a standard defence, outlier rejection: discard, pixel by pixel, the values that disagree with the other exposures. Proper coaddition as written has none.
This is not a thought experiment. In our real data one exposure was taken during a gust of wind and shows every star twice. Its PSF fit looked perfectly normal, it was coadded with the others, and a ghost star appeared in the result.
Making the estimator robust, so that an exposure or a pixel that contradicts the others is detected and set aside, without giving up what proper coaddition gains, is the first task of the project. It requires replacing the square in the least-squares criterion by something more tolerant, and then there is no closed form any more. Notebook 9 provides the tools.

title: 9  Iterative methods: when there is no closed form
text:
9.1 Operators, not matrices
This notebook follows chapter 4 of H. Talbot’s Lecture Notes on Optimisation (gradient descent, conjugate gradient, majorise-minimise) and applies it to the problems of the previous notebooks. It is the bridge from the textbook material to the research project.
Every solution so far was a formula: transform, divide with care, transform back. That works when a fast transform diagonalises the problem and the criterion is a sum of squares. Change either, and the formula is gone: a blur that varies across the image, boundaries that are neither periodic nor reflexive, a penalty that is not quadratic (notebook 7), a loss that must resist outliers (notebook 8).
What you will take away
An iterative method never asks “what is \(A\)?”. It asks “what is \(A\) times this vector?”, and sometimes “what is \(A^{\mathsf T}\) times that one?”. So we write the blur as two functions. For a convolution, \(A^{\mathsf T}\) is the convolution with the PSF flipped upside-down and left-right; in Fourier space, multiplication by the conjugate \(\bar K\).
We keep the FFT here because it is fast and familiar, but nothing below depends on it: replace the bodies of A and AT by any linear operation and its transpose, and the algorithms are unchanged.
x_true = data['hubble'].astype(float)
K = hno.psf2otf(hno.gaussian_psf(x_true.shape, fwhm=6.0))

A = lambda v: ifft2(K * fft2(v)).real                  # blur
AT = lambda v: ifft2(np.conj(K) * fft2(v)).real        # its transpose

b = A(x_true) + 0.005 * rng.standard_normal(x_true.shape)
A habit worth more than any algorithm: test your transpose. By definition, \(\langle A u, v\rangle = \langle u, A^{\mathsf T} v\rangle\) for all \(u, v\). Take two random images and compare the two numbers. If they differ, the operator pair is wrong, and every method built on it will quietly converge to nonsense.
u, v = rng.standard_normal(x_true.shape), rng.standard_normal(x_true.shape)
print('<A u, v>  =', np.sum(A(u) * v))
print('<u, AT v> =', np.sum(u * AT(v)))

<u, AT v> = 49.15959985748253

title: 9  Iterative methods: when there is no closed form
text:
9.2 Gradient descent
Take the plain least-squares criterion \(F(x) = \tfrac12 \|A x - b\|^2\). Its gradient is \(\nabla F(x) = A^{\mathsf T}(A x - b)\): blur the current guess, compare with the data, send the difference back through \(A^{\mathsf T}\). Gradient descent walks downhill,
\[x_{k+1} = x_k - \tau\, A^{\mathsf T}(A x_k - b) ,\]
and converges if the step \(\tau\) is below \(2 / \|A\|^2\). For a blur that conserves light the largest singular value is 1, so \(\tau = 1\) is safe.

x = np.zeros_like(b)
err_gd = []
for k in range(1500):
    x = x - 1.0 * AT(A(x) - b)
    err_gd.append(hno.rel_error(x, x_true))
k_best = int(np.argmin(err_gd)) + 1

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.1))
ax.loglog(np.arange(1, 1501), err_gd, color=hno.BLUE)
ax.plot(k_best, min(err_gd), 'o', color=hno.ORANGE)
ax.axhline(hno.rel_error(b, x_true), color=hno.INK2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 2)))
ax.text(1, hno.rel_error(b, x_true) * 1.04, 'blurred data', fontsize=8, color=hno.INK2)
ax.set_xlabel('iteration'); ax.set_ylabel('relative error'); ax.set_title('Gradient descent on the unregularised problem', loc='left');
print(f'smallest error {min(err_gd):.4f} at iteration {k_best};  after 1500 iterations {err_gd[-1]:.4f}')

smallest error 0.0271 at iteration 56;  after 1500 iterations 0.0556








Figure 9.1: Gradient descent on the unregularised problem: the error decreases, then increases again.





In Figure 9.1 the error goes down, reaches a minimum, and comes back up. We are minimising the unregularised criterion, whose minimiser is the naive solution of notebook 1; given enough iterations, gradient descent would get there, garbage included.
But it gets there in a particular order. One can show that after \(k\) steps the iterate is a filtered solution in the sense of notebook 5, with filter factors \(\phi_i = 1 - (1 - \tau\sigma_i^2)^k\): the components with large singular values converge first, the noisy ones last. Stopping early is a regularisation, and the iteration count plays the role of \(1/\alpha\). This behaviour is called semi-convergence. It is the U-curve once more, with the iteration number on the horizontal axis.

title: 9  Iterative methods: when there is no closed form
text:
9.3 Conjugate gradient
Now a criterion with a proper minimum: Tikhonov, \(F(x) = \tfrac12\|Ax - b\|^2
+ \tfrac12\alpha^2\|x\|^2\). Its minimiser solves the regularised normal equations of notebook 6,
\[\underbrace{(A^{\mathsf T} A + \alpha^2 I)}_{M}\; x = A^{\mathsf T} b ,\]
a linear system whose matrix \(M\) is symmetric positive definite. For such systems there is a method far better than gradient descent. Gradient descent forgets where it has been and keeps partially undoing its previous steps. Conjugate gradient (CG) chooses each new direction so that it never spoils what the previous directions achieved. It needs one product by \(M\) per iteration, like gradient descent, and nothing else.

def conjugate_gradient(M, rhs, iterations, callback=None):
    """Solve M x = rhs for a symmetric positive definite operator M (a function)."""
    x = np.zeros_like(rhs)
    r = rhs - M(x)                         # residual
    p = r.copy()                           # search direction
    rs = np.sum(r * r)
    for _ in range(iterations):
        Mp = M(p)
        step = rs / np.sum(p * Mp)
        x = x + step * p
        r = r - step * Mp
        rs_new = np.sum(r * r)
        p = r + (rs_new / rs) * p          # new direction, conjugate to the previous ones
        rs = rs_new
        if callback: callback(x)
    return x

alpha = 0.05
M = lambda v: AT(A(v)) + alpha**2 * v
rhs = AT(b)
x_formula = ifft2(np.conj(K) * fft2(b) / (np.abs(K)**2 + alpha**2)).real    # the filter of notebook 6

dist_cg, dist_gd = [], []
conjugate_gradient(M, rhs, 60, callback=lambda x: dist_cg.append(hno.rel_error(x, x_formula)))
x = np.zeros_like(b)
for k in range(60):
    x = x - (M(x) - rhs) / (1 + alpha**2)
    dist_gd.append(hno.rel_error(x, x_formula))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.1))
ax.semilogy(np.arange(1, 61), dist_gd, color=hno.ORANGE, label='gradient descent')
ax.semilogy(np.arange(1, 61), dist_cg, color=hno.BLUE, label='conjugate gradient')
ax.set_xlabel('iteration'); ax.set_ylabel('distance to the exact Tikhonov solution'); ax.legend()
ax.set_title('Same cost per iteration, very different progress', loc='left');
print(f'after 60 iterations: gradient descent {dist_gd[-1]:.1e},  conjugate gradient {dist_cg[-1]:.1e}')

after 60 iterations: gradient descent 1.7e-02,  conjugate gradient 1.5e-04








Figure 9.2: Distance to the exact Tikhonov solution, for gradient descent and for conjugate gradient.





Here we could check the answer, because for this problem the formula exists. The point of CG is that it does not need the formula: give it any pair A, AT and it solves the Tikhonov problem, for the penalties of notebook 7 as well. It is the workhorse of large inverse problems.

title: 9  Iterative methods: when there is no closed form
text:
9.4 Majorise-minimise
Gradient descent and CG handle smooth criteria; CG wants a quadratic one. For anything else there is a strategy of great generality.

To minimise a difficult function \(F\), replace it by an easy function \(Q\) that lies above \(F\) everywhere and touches it at the current point. Minimise \(Q\). Repeat.

Since \(Q \ge F\) with equality at the current point, the minimiser of \(Q\) can only have a lower (or equal) value of \(F\): the criterion decreases at every step, with no step size to tune. The art is in choosing \(Q\) quadratic, so that each step is a least-squares problem we already know how to solve.
A one-number example. Notebook 8 ended with a satellite trail. Look at a single pixel on the trail, through the 45 exposures: 44 values scattered around the truth and one far off. We want the “typical” value.

Least squares, \(\sum_i (y_i - m)^2\), gives the mean, which the outlier drags away.
A robust loss grows quadratically for small residuals and only linearly for large ones, so an outlier cannot pull as hard. The classical choice is Huber’s, \[\rho(r) = \begin{cases} r^2/2 & |r| \le \delta \\ \delta\,|r| - \delta^2/2 & |r| > \delta . \end{cases}\]


delta = 2.5
huber = lambda r: np.where(np.abs(r) <= delta, 0.5 * r**2, delta * np.abs(r) - 0.5 * delta**2)
clip = lambda r: np.clip(r, -delta, delta)                 # the derivative of the Huber loss

values = 1.0 + 0.1 * rng.standard_normal(45)               # one pixel in 45 exposures, noise 0.1
values[10] += 3.0                                          # ... one of them on the trail
sigma = 0.1

F = lambda m: np.sum(huber((values - m) / sigma))
m = values.mean()                                          # start from the least-squares answer
path = [m]
for _ in range(6):
    r = (values - m) / sigma
    m = np.mean(m + sigma * clip(r))                       # mean of the "modified" data: one MM step
    path.append(m)

grid_m = np.linspace(0.9, 1.15, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.3))
ax.plot(grid_m, [F(g) for g in grid_m], color=hno.BLUE, label='robust criterion $F(m)$')
for k, col in ((0, hno.ORANGE), (1, hno.AQUA)):
    mk = path[k]; rk = (values - mk) / sigma
    Q = [F(mk) + np.sum(-clip(rk) * (g - mk) / sigma) + 0.5 * len(values) * ((g - mk) / sigma)**2 for g in grid_m]
    ax.plot(grid_m, Q, color=col, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label=f'quadratic majoriser at step {k}')
    ax.plot(mk, F(mk), 'o', color=col)
ax.set_ylim(F(path[-1]) - 3, F(path[0]) + 12); ax.set_xlabel('estimate $m$'); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title('Majorise-minimise on one pixel', loc='left');
print(f'mean (least squares): {values.mean():.3f}     robust estimate: {path[-1]:.3f}     median: {np.median(values):.3f}     truth: 1.000')
print('iterates:', np.round(path, 4))

mean (least squares): 1.065     robust estimate: 1.004     median: 1.005     truth: 1.000
iterates: [1.0651 1.005  1.0037 1.0036 1.0036 1.0036 1.0036]








Figure 9.3: Majorise-minimise on one pixel: the robust criterion and two quadratic majorisers.





In Figure 9.3 each dashed parabola lies above the blue curve and touches it at the current estimate; its minimum is the next estimate. Two steps are enough here.
Look at what one step is. The Huber loss has curvature at most 1, so the parabola of curvature 1 tangent to it at the current residual \(r_k\) is a majoriser. Minimising a sum of such parabolas is a least-squares problem, on modified data: each value is kept if its residual is small, and pulled back to within \(\delta\) noise levels of the current estimate if it is not,
\[y_i' = m_k + \sigma\,\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{y_i - m_k}{\sigma}\right) .\]
The outlier is not deleted by a rule; it is limited in how much it can disagree, and it finds its own place as the iterations proceed.
(Notebook 7 used the other common majoriser, for the absolute value: \(|t| \le t^2 / (2|t_k|) + |t_k|/2\), which gives a re-weighted least-squares problem at each step.)

title: 9  Iterative methods: when there is no closed form
text:
9.5 Robust proper coaddition
Now the whole image. Replace the square by the Huber loss in the criterion of notebook 8:
\[\hat x = \arg\min_x \;\sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{\text{pixels}} \rho\!\left(\frac{y_i - k_i * x}{s_i}\right) .\]
The majorise-minimise step is exactly the one above, exposure by exposure and pixel by pixel:

predict every exposure from the current estimate: \(k_i * x_k\);
clip the residuals: \(\;y_i' = k_i * x_k + s_i\,\mathrm{clip}\bigl((y_i - k_i * x_k)/s_i\bigr)\);
solve the least-squares problem for the modified exposures. That is an ordinary proper coaddition, the three-line formula of notebook 8.

So the robust estimator costs a few proper coadditions, and reuses all of the code. Here is the simulation of notebook 8 again, satellite trail included.

P = data['all_psf'].astype(float)
noise = P[:, 6] / P[:, 7]

def frame_otf(shape, p, zoom=1.0):
    Kf = hno.psf2otf(hno.moffat_psf(shape, p[0] * zoom, p[1] * zoom, p[2], p[3]))
    nu_y, nu_x = fftfreq(shape[0])[:, None], fftfreq(shape[1])[None, :]
    return Kf * np.exp(-2j * np.pi * (nu_x * p[4] * zoom + nu_y * p[5] * zoom))

def coadd_solve(Y, Ks, s, lam):
    """Proper coaddition without the target: the least-squares solution X."""
    w = (1.0 / s**2)[:, None, None]
    S = np.sum(w * np.abs(Ks)**2, axis=0)
    return np.sum(w * np.conj(Ks) * Y, axis=0) / (S + lam * S.flat[0])

def robust_coadd(y, Ks, s, lam, delta=2.5, iterations=5):
    """Huber-loss proper coaddition by majorise-minimise. y: exposures (N, h, w)."""
    X = coadd_solve(fft2(y), Ks, s, lam)                       # start: ordinary proper coaddition
    for _ in range(iterations):
        predicted = ifft2(Ks * X).real
        r = (y - predicted) / s[:, None, None]
        X = coadd_solve(fft2(predicted + s[:, None, None] * np.clip(r, -delta, delta)), Ks, s, lam)
    return X, np.abs(r) > delta                                # solution, and which residuals were clipped

sim_rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
Ks = np.array([frame_otf(x_true.shape, p, zoom=2.0) for p in P])
s = 0.05 * noise / np.median(noise)
y = np.array([ifft2(Kf * fft2(x_true)).real + si * sim_rng.standard_normal(x_true.shape) for Kf, si in zip(Ks, s)])
yy, xx = np.indices(x_true.shape)
y[10] += 3.0 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((yy - 0.45 * xx - 60) / 1.5)**2)          # the satellite trail, in exposure 10

T = hno.psf2otf(hno.gaussian_psf(x_true.shape, 2 * 2.36)).real
truth = ifft2(T * fft2(x_true)).real
core = (slice(24, -24), slice(24, -24))
error = lambda X: hno.rel_error(ifft2(T * X).real[core] - truth[core].mean(), truth[core] - truth[core].mean())

lam = 3e-3
X_plain = coadd_solve(fft2(y), Ks, s, lam)
X_robust, clipped = robust_coadd(y, Ks, s, lam)
print(f'ordinary proper coaddition : error {error(X_plain):.4f}')
print(f'robust proper coaddition   : error {error(X_robust):.4f}      (without any trail: 0.0228)')
print(f'residuals clipped: {clipped.mean():.2%} of all pixels;  in exposure 10: {clipped[10].mean():.2%}')

hno.show([ifft2(T * X_plain).real, ifft2(T * X_robust).real, clipped[10].astype(float)],
         ['ordinary proper coaddition', 'robust proper coaddition', 'clipped pixels of exposure 10'], width=3.3);

ordinary proper coaddition : error 0.0427
robust proper coaddition   : error 0.0228      (without any trail: 0.0228)
residuals clipped: 1.29% of all pixels;  in exposure 10: 4.16%








Figure 9.4: Ordinary and robust proper coaddition of the simulation with a satellite trail, and the pixels of the spoiled exposure that were clipped.





The trail is gone and the error is back to its value without any trail. The third panel shows which pixels of the spoiled exposure were limited: the estimator found the trail by itself, because those pixels disagreed with what the 44 other exposures said about the sky. Everything else in that exposure was kept and used.
About 1.2 % of the pixels of every clean exposure are clipped too: with \(\delta = 2.5\), that is the share of ordinary Gaussian noise beyond 2.5 standard deviations. Clipping them costs a little efficiency; it is the insurance premium.

text:
9.6 Real data: the robust loss as a diagnostic
On the real exposures nobody added a trail. But run the robust estimator anyway and ask where the residuals are clipped. Wherever many exposures disagree with the model at the same place, the model is wrong there.

cube = data['cube'].astype(float)
N, shape = len(cube), cube.shape[1:]
K_real = np.array([frame_otf(shape, p) for p in P])
pixel_noise = np.array([1.4826 * np.median(np.abs((cube[i] - cube[(i + 1) % N]) - np.median(cube[i] - cube[(i + 1) % N]))) / np.sqrt(2) for i in range(N)])
tapered = np.array([hno.taper(f, 12) for f in cube])

X_real, clipped_real = robust_coadd(tapered, K_real, pixel_noise, 3e-3, iterations=15)
how_often = clipped_real.mean(axis=0)                        # per pixel: fraction of exposures clipped
print(f'clipped overall: {clipped_real.mean():.2%}   (pure Gaussian noise would give 1.24 %)')
print(f'pixels clipped in more than half of the exposures: {(how_often > 0.5).mean():.2%} of the image')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.6, 3.6))
m = cube.mean(axis=0); lo, hi = np.percentile(m, [1, 99.7])
ax[0].imshow(np.clip((m - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1) ** 0.5); ax[0].set_title('mean of the 45 exposures')
im = ax[1].imshow(how_often, cmap='gray_r', vmin=0, vmax=0.6); ax[1].set_title('how often each pixel was clipped')
for a in ax:
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); a.grid(False)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], fraction=0.046, label='fraction of exposures'); fig.tight_layout()

clipped overall: 2.95%   (pure Gaussian noise would give 1.24 %)
pixels clipped in more than half of the exposures: 0.88% of the image








Figure 9.5: The mean of the real exposures, and how often each pixel was clipped by the robust estimator.





The map of Figure 9.5 is nearly white on the nebula, where the model holds and only the expected share of noise is clipped, and dark on the stars. This is the model violation we have met in every notebook since the first, now located automatically: a saturated core that is not the sky convolved with the PSF, and PSF wings that a Moffat profile does not describe exactly.
A robust loss is therefore two things at once: a protection against bad data, and an instrument that shows where the model and the data part company.

text:
9.7 Where the project starts
You now have the full chain: the model of a blurred image, its fast solution, the reason regularisation is unavoidable and how to choose it, the extension to many exposures, and the tools to go beyond least squares. The research project begins exactly at the edge of what this notebook showed. Some of the questions it leaves open:

A whole exposure can be wrong, not just some of its pixels: the exposure with doubled stars in our real data has a wrong PSF. Is the pixel-wise Huber loss enough, or do we need a test per exposure? What should that test measure?
How should \(\delta\) be chosen, and can the star cores be protected from being clipped merely because they are bright and imperfectly modelled?
Does robustness cost resolution or noise on clean data? Notebook 8 gave the tools to measure both, on real exposures, with error bars.
Does the declared-target contract survive? The delivered PSF must still be verified on the stars of the result.
Convergence and cost on full-size images of sixty million pixels and two hundred exposures.

None of these has a textbook answer. That is what makes it research.

Break the transpose. Replace np.conj(K) by K in AT and run the test of section 9.1, then conjugate gradient. What happens? Why did it make no difference for the Gaussian PSF, and why would it for our tilted telescope PSF?

Plot \(\phi\) against \(\sigma\) for \(k = 10, 100, 1000\) next to the Tikhonov filter. Which \(\alpha\) does each \(k\) resemble?

"""Small helpers shared by the notebooks. Read this file: it is short, and
everything in it is something you should be able to write yourself."""
import os
import numpy as np
from numpy.fft import fft2, ifft2, ifftshift, fftfreq
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA = '#2a78d6', '#eb6834', '#1baf7a'
INK, INK2, SURFACE, GRIDC = '#0b0b0b', '#52514e', '#fcfcfb', '#e4e3df'


def style():
    """One plotting style for the whole series."""
    plt.rcParams.update({
        'figure.facecolor': SURFACE, 'axes.facecolor': SURFACE, 'savefig.facecolor': SURFACE,
        'axes.edgecolor': GRIDC, 'axes.labelcolor': INK2, 'text.color': INK,
        'xtick.color': INK2, 'ytick.color': INK2, 'axes.grid': True, 'grid.color': GRIDC,
        'grid.linewidth': 0.6, 'axes.spines.top': False, 'axes.spines.right': False,
        'font.size': 9, 'axes.titlesize': 9.5, 'lines.linewidth': 2.0,
        'legend.frameon': False, 'figure.dpi': 110, 'image.cmap': 'gray',
        'image.interpolation': 'nearest'})


def load_sample():
    """The real-data sample (see make_sample.py for what each array is)."""
    here = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
    return dict(np.load(os.path.join(here, 'data', 'm16_sample.npz')))


def gaussian_psf(shape, fwhm):
    """Circular Gaussian PSF, centred on the array, summing to 1."""
    sigma = fwhm / (2 * np.sqrt(2 * np.log(2)))
    y, x = np.indices(shape)
    y, x = y - shape[0] // 2, x - shape[1] // 2
    p = np.exp(-(x**2 + y**2) / (2 * sigma**2))
    return p / p.sum()


def moffat_psf(shape, fwhm_major, fwhm_minor=None, pa_deg=0.0, beta=2.5):
    """Elliptical Moffat PSF, the usual model of a star seen through the
    atmosphere: (1 + r^2)^(-beta), heavier wings than a Gaussian."""
    fwhm_minor = fwhm_minor or fwhm_major
    c = 2 * np.sqrt(2 ** (1 / beta) - 1)          # FWHM = c * alpha
    a, b = fwhm_major / c, fwhm_minor / c
    y, x = np.indices(shape)
    y, x = y - shape[0] // 2, x - shape[1] // 2
    t = np.radians(pa_deg)
    u = (x * np.cos(t) + y * np.sin(t)) / a
    v = (-x * np.sin(t) + y * np.cos(t)) / b
    p = (1 + u**2 + v**2) ** (-beta)
    return p / p.sum()


def psf2otf(psf):
    """Fourier transform of a centred PSF (its optical transfer function)."""
    return fft2(ifftshift(psf))


def blur(x, psf):
    """Convolve x with psf, with periodic boundaries (one FFT product)."""
    return np.real(ifft2(fft2(x) * psf2otf(psf)))


def radial_profile(a):
    """Azimuthal average of a 2-D Fourier-domain array (fft2 layout).
    Returns frequency in cycles/pixel and the averaged values."""
    n0, n1 = a.shape
    r = np.hypot(fftfreq(n0)[:, None], fftfreq(n1)[None, :])
    idx = np.rint(r * max(n0, n1)).astype(int)
    nb = max(n0, n1) // 2 + 1
    tot = np.bincount(idx.ravel(), weights=np.abs(a).ravel(), minlength=nb)[:nb]
    cnt = np.bincount(idx.ravel(), minlength=nb)[:nb]
    return np.arange(nb) / max(n0, n1), tot / np.maximum(cnt, 1)


def rel_error(estimate, truth):
    """Relative error ||estimate - truth|| / ||truth||."""
    return np.linalg.norm(estimate - truth) / np.linalg.norm(truth)


def show(images, titles=None, lo=1, hi=99.7, same_scale=False, width=3.0, gamma=0.5):
    """Show images side by side with a percentile stretch.
    same_scale=True uses the first image's limits for all of them."""
    images = list(images)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(images), figsize=(width * len(images), width * 1.08), squeeze=False)
    lim = None
    for ax, im, k in zip(axes[0], images, range(len(images))):
        if lim is None or not same_scale:
            lim = np.percentile(im, [lo, hi])
        z = np.clip((im - lim[0]) / (lim[1] - lim[0] + 1e-30), 0, 1) ** gamma
        ax.imshow(z, vmin=0, vmax=1)
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
        for sp in ax.spines.values():
            sp.set_visible(False)
        if titles:
            ax.set_title(titles[k])
    fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
    return fig


def find_stars(img, n=10, box=9):
    """Positions (row, col) and peak values of the n brightest local maxima,
    brightest first. Good enough to locate stars in a small field."""
    from scipy import ndimage
    smooth = ndimage.gaussian_filter(img, 1.0)
    peak = (smooth == ndimage.maximum_filter(smooth, box))
    peak[:box, :] = peak[-box:, :] = False
    peak[:, :box] = peak[:, -box:] = False
    rows, cols = np.nonzero(peak)
    order = np.argsort(img[rows, cols])[::-1][:n]
    return [(int(rows[i]), int(cols[i]), float(img[rows[i], cols[i]])) for i in order]


def lecture_signal(N=250):
    """The 1-D test signal of H. Talbot's lecture notes (notebook 1):
    steps plus slow waves, sampled on [0, 3 pi]. Returns (abscissa, signal)."""
    s = np.linspace(0, 3 * np.pi, N)
    return s, 1.0 * (np.cos(2 * s) > 0) + 2 * np.sin(s / 4) + 0.1 * np.cos(3 * s + 1)


def gaussian_kernel_1d(sigma, half):
    """Normalised 1-D Gaussian kernel of 2*half + 1 samples."""
    o = np.arange(-half, half + 1)
    k = np.exp(-o**2 / (2 * sigma**2))
    return k / k.sum()


def blur_matrix_1d(kernel, N, mode='constant'):
    """Blurring matrix of a signal of length N (notebook 4): one column per
    sample. mode = 'constant' (zero), 'wrap' (periodic) or 'reflect'."""
    from scipy import ndimage
    return np.column_stack([ndimage.convolve1d(np.eye(N)[j], kernel, mode=mode) for j in range(N)])


# ---- reflexive boundaries: the cosine transform (notebook 4) ----

def dct2(a):
    from scipy.fft import dctn
    return dctn(a, type=2, norm='ortho')


def idct2(a):
    from scipy.fft import idctn
    return idctn(a, type=2, norm='ortho')


def dct_eigenvalues(psf, shape):
    """Eigenvalues of the blur with reflexive boundaries, for a PSF that is
    symmetric in both directions: dct2(A e1) / dct2(e1)."""
    from scipy import ndimage
    e1 = np.zeros(shape); e1[0, 0] = 1.0
    return dct2(ndimage.convolve(e1, psf, mode='reflect')) / dct2(e1)


def make_test_problem(big, psf, noise, margin=64, seed=1):
    """Honest test data (notebook 4): blur a large scene, keep its centre,
    add noise. Returns (x_true, b)."""
    from scipy import ndimage
    inner = slice(margin, big.shape[0] - margin)
    blurred = ndimage.convolve(big, psf, mode='reflect')[inner, inner]
    return big[inner, inner], blurred + noise * np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(blurred.shape)


def taper(b, width=16):
    """Fade an image to its mean over `width` pixels along every edge, so
    that periodic boundaries do no harm (notebook 4)."""
    ry, rx = np.ones(b.shape[0]), np.ones(b.shape[1])
    edge = 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(np.pi * np.arange(width) / width)
    for r in (ry, rx):
        r[:width] = edge; r[-width:] = edge[::-1]
    return b.mean() + (b - b.mean()) * np.outer(ry, rx)


def fit_star(img, row, col, half=10):
    """Fit a circular Moffat profile on a constant background to the star
    near (row, col) (notebook 3). Returns a dict with the FWHM in pixels."""
    from scipy import optimize
    stamp = img[row - half:row + half + 1, col - half:col + half + 1]
    yy, xx = np.indices(stamp.shape) - half
    def model(p):
        amp, y0, x0, alpha, beta, bg = p
        return bg + amp * (1 + ((yy - y0)**2 + (xx - x0)**2) / alpha**2) ** (-beta)
    span = stamp.max() - np.median(stamp)
    fit = optimize.least_squares(lambda p: (model(p) - stamp).ravel(),
                                 x0=[span, 0, 0, 3.0, 2.5, np.median(stamp)],
                                 bounds=([0, -3, -3, 0.3, 1.1, -np.inf], [10 * span + 1e-30, 3, 3, 30, 50, np.inf]))
    amp, y0, x0, alpha, beta, bg = fit.x
    return {'fwhm': 2 * alpha * np.sqrt(2 ** (1 / beta) - 1), 'beta': beta, 'amp': amp,
            'bg': bg, 'row': row + y0, 'col': col + x0}
